1.4.oldText: 3. I have a scrupulosity peculiar to myself, which I confess reluctantly — it concerns morality. It showed itself in my life so early, so spontaneously, so persistently, and in such keen opposition to environment, epoch, precedent and ancestry, that I would almost be entitled to call it my "â priori." So my curiosity and my suspicion were early bound to halt at the question of what the origin of our "Good" and our "Evil" actually was. Indeed, at the boyish age of thirteen the problem of the origin of Evil already haunted me. At an age "when games and God divide one's heart," I devoted my first childish attempt at the literary game, my first philosophic essay, to that problem. As for my childish solution, well, I quite properly gave the honor to God and made him the father of evil. Did my own "â priori" demand that solution from me? That new, immoral, or at least "amoral" "â priori," and the "categorical imperative" which was its voice (but oh! how hostile to the Kantian article, and how pregnant with problems!), has had more and more of my attention since then, and indeed more than attention. Fortunately I soon learned to separate theological from moral prejudices, and I gave up looking for a supernatural origin of evil. A certain amount of historical and philological education, to say nothing of an innate faculty of psychological discrimination par excellence, almost immediately transformed my original problem into the following one: Under what conditions did Man invent for himself those judgments of values, "Good" and "Evil"? And what intrinsic value do they have in themselves? Have they so far hindered or advanced human well-being? Are they a symptom of the distress, impoverishment and degeneration of Human Life? Or, conversely, do the fullness, the strength and the will of Life, its courage, its self-confidence, its future, show themselves in them? On this point I found and hazarded in my mind the most diverse answers. I established distinctions among periods, peoples and castes, and I became a specialist in my problem. From my answers grew new questions, new investigations, new conjectures, new probabilities, until at last I had a land of my own and a soil of my own, a whole secret world growing and flowering, like hidden gardens whose existence no one could have an inkling of. Oh, how happy we are, we finders of knowledge, provided that we know how to keep silent long enough.

1.5.oldText: 4. I owe my first impulse to publish some of my hypotheses on the origin of morality to a clear, well-written and even precocious little book. In it a perverse and vicious kind of moral philosophy (your real English kind) was presented to me definitely for the first time. It attracted me with that magnetic attraction which belongs to whatever is diametrically opposed and antithetical to one's own ideas. The title of the book was The Origin of the Moral Emotions; its author was Dr. Paul Rée; the year of its appearance was 1877. I may almost say that I have never read anything in which every single dogma and conclusion called forth from me so emphatic a negation as in that book — though it was a negation tainted by either pique or intolerance. In the works on which I was then working I therefore referred, in season and out of season, to the arguments of that book. I did not mean to refute them — for what have I to do with mere refutations? As is natural to a positive mind, I substituted a more probable theory for an improbable one, and occasionally, no doubt, one philosophic error for another. In that early period I gave, as I have said, the first public expression to the theories of origin to which these essays are devoted. I did it with a clumsiness that I was the last to conceal from myself, for I was still cramped, still without a special language for these special subjects, and still frequently liable to relapse and vacillation. For details, compare what I say in Human, all-too-Human, part i., about the parallel early history of Good and Evil, Aph. 45 (namely, their origin from the castes of the aristocrats and the slaves); similarly, Aph. 136 et seq., on the birth and value of ascetic morality; similarly, Aphs. 96, 99, vol. ii., Aph. 89, on the Morality of Custom, that far older and more original kind of morality which is toto cœlo different from the altruistic ethics (in which Dr. Rée, like all the English moral philosophers, sees the ethical "Thing-in-itself"); finally, Aph. 92. Similarly, Aph. 26 in Human, all-too-Human, part ii., and Aph. 112, the Dawn of Day, on the origin of Justice as a balance between persons of approximately equal power (equilibrium as the hypothesis of all contract, and consequently of all law); similarly, on the origin of Punishment, Human, all-too-Human, part ii., Aphs. 22, 23, on which point the deterrent object is neither essential nor original (as Dr. Rée thinks: rather this object is only imported, under certain definite conditions, and always as something extra and additional).

1.6.oldText: 5. In reality I had set my heart at that time on something much more important than the theories, mine or others', about the origin of morality (or, more precisely, the real function of these theories, from my view, was to point to an end to which they were one means among many). The issue for me was the value of morality, and on that subject I had to place myself in a state of abstraction in which I was almost alone with my great teacher Schopenhauer, to whom that book, with all its passion and inherent contradiction (for that book also was a polemic), turned for present help as though he were still alive. The issue was, strangely enough, the value of the "un-egoistic" instincts, the instincts of pity, self-denial and self-sacrifice, which Schopenhauer had so persistently painted in golden colors, deified and etherealized, that eventually they seemed to him, as it were, high and dry, "intrinsic values in themselves," on the strength of which he uttered his own negation, both to Life and to himself. But against these very instincts a more and more fundamental mistrust voiced itself in my soul, a skepticism that dug ever deeper and deeper. In this very instinct I saw the great danger of mankind, its most sublime temptation and seduction — seduction to what? to nothingness? In these very instincts I saw the beginning of the end, stability, the exhaustion that gazes backwards, the will turning against Life, the last illness announcing itself with its own mincing melancholy. I realized that the morality of pity, which spread wider and wider and whose grip infected even philosophers with its disease, was the most sinister symptom of our modern European civilization. I realized that it was the route along which that civilization slid on its way to — a new Buddhism? — a European Buddhism? — Nihilism? This exaggerated estimation in which modern philosophers have held pity is quite a new phenomenon: up to that time philosophers were absolutely unanimous about the worthlessness of pity. I need only mention Plato, Spinoza, La Rochefoucauld and Kant — four minds as different from each other as is possible, but united on one point: their contempt of pity.

1.7.oldText: 6. This problem of the value of pity and of the pity-morality (I am an opponent of the modern infamous emasculation of our emotions) seems at first blush a mere isolated problem, a note of interrogation standing by itself. But whoever once halts at this problem and learns how to put questions will experience what I experienced. A new and immense vista unfolds before him, a sense of potentiality seizes him like a vertigo, every species of doubt, mistrust and fear springs up, the belief in morality, nay, in all morality, totters — and finally a new demand voices itself. Let us speak out this new demand: we need a critique of moral values, and the value of these values is to be called into question for the first time. For this we need a knowledge of the conditions and circumstances out of which these values grew, under which they evolved and became distorted (morality as a result, as a symptom, as a mask, as Tartuffism, as disease, as a misunderstanding; but also morality as a cause, as a remedy, as a stimulant, as a fetter, as a drug). We need it all the more because such a knowledge has neither existed until now nor is even now generally desired. The value of these "values" was taken for granted as an indisputable fact, beyond all question. No one has shown the faintest doubt or hesitation, until now, in judging the "good man" to be of higher value than the "evil man" — higher value specifically for human progress, utility and prosperity generally, not forgetting the future. What? Suppose the converse were the truth! What? Suppose there lurked in the "good man" a symptom of retrogression, such as a danger, a temptation, a poison, a narcotic, by means of which the present battened on the future! More comfortable and less risky perhaps than its opposite, but also pettier, meaner! So that morality would really be saddled with the guilt, if the maximum potentiality of the power and splendor of the human species were never to be attained? So that really morality would be the danger of dangers?

1.8.oldText: 7. Enough: after this vista had disclosed itself to me, I had reason to search for learned, bold and industrious colleagues (I am doing it even to this very day). It means traversing the immense, distant and completely unexplored land of morality with new clamorous questions and at the same time with new eyes — a morality which has actually existed and been actually lived! And is this not practically equivalent to first discovering that land? If I thought, among others, of the aforesaid Dr. Rée in this context, I did so because I had no doubt that the very nature of his questions would compel him to have recourse to a truer method in order to obtain his answers. Have I deceived myself on that score? At all events I wished to give a better direction of vision to an eye of such keenness and such impartiality. I wished to direct him to the real history of morality, and to warn him, while there was yet time, against a world of English theories that culminated in the blue vacuum of heaven. Other colors, of course, rise immediately to one's mind as being a hundred times more potent than blue for a genealogy of morals: for instance, gray, by which I mean authentic facts capable of definite proof and actually existing — or, to put it shortly, the whole of that long hieroglyphic script (so hard to decipher) of the past history of human morals. This script was unknown to Dr. Rée; but he had read Darwin. And so in his philosophy the Darwinian beast and that pink of modernity, the demure weakling and dilettante who "bites no longer," shake hands politely, in a fashion that is at least instructive. The latter wears a certain facial expression of refined and good-humored indolence, tinged with a touch of pessimism and exhaustion, as if it really did not pay to take all these things — I mean moral problems — so seriously. I, on the other hand, think that there are no subjects which pay better for being taken seriously; part of this payment is that perhaps eventually they admit of being taken gaily. This gaiety, or, to use my own language, this joyful wisdom, is indeed a payment — a payment for a protracted, brave, laborious and burrowing seriousness, which, it goes without saying, is the attribute of but a few. But on the day when we say from the fullness of our hearts, "Forward! our old morality too is fit material for Comedy," we shall have discovered a new plot and a new possibility for the Dionysian drama entitled The Soul's Fate — and he will speedily make use of it, one can safely wager, he, the great ancient eternal dramatist of the comedy of our existence.

1.9.oldText: 8. If this writing is obscure to anyone and jars on his ears, I do not think that I am necessarily to blame. It is clear enough on the hypothesis I presuppose, namely that the reader has first read my previous writings and has not grudged them a certain amount of trouble: it is not, indeed, a simple matter to get at their essence. Take, for instance, my Zarathustra. I allow no one to pass as knowing that book unless every single word in it has at some time wounded him profoundly and at some time enchanted him profoundly. Then, and not till then, can he enjoy the privilege of reverently sharing in the halcyon element from which that work is born, in its sunny brilliance, its distance, its spaciousness, its certainty. In other cases the aphoristic form produces difficulty, but this is only because the form is treated too casually. An aphorism properly coined and cast into its final mold is far from being "deciphered" as soon as it has been read; on the contrary, that is when it first requires to be expounded — and for that an art of exposition is of course necessary. The third essay in this book provides an example of what I call exposition in such cases: an aphorism is prefixed to that essay, and the essay itself is its commentary. One quality is certainly essential in order to practise reading as an art, and it has nowadays been best forgotten — that is why it will take some time yet for my writings to become readable. It is a quality for which one must be a cow, and under no circumstances a modern man! — rumination.

2.3.oldText: 2. All honor, then, to the noble spirits who would gladly dominate these historians of morality. But it is certainly a pity that they themselves lack the historical sense, and that all the beneficent spirits of history have deserted them. The whole train of their thought runs, as it always did with old-fashioned philosophers, along thoroughly unhistorical lines; there is no doubt of this. The crass ineptitude of their genealogy of morals shows at once when the question is the origin of the idea and judgment of "good." "Originally," so runs their decree, "man praised altruistic acts and called them 'good' from the standpoint of those on whom they were conferred, that is, those to whom they were useful. Later the origin of this praise was forgotten, and altruistic acts, simply because they were habitually praised as good, also came to be felt as good, as though they contained some intrinsic goodness." The thing is obvious: this first derivation already contains all the typical and peculiar traits of the English psychologists. We have "utility," "forgetting," "habit," and finally "error," the whole assemblage forming the basis of a system of values, of which the higher man has until now been proud, as though it were a privilege of man in general. This pride must be brought low, this system of values must lose its value: is that achieved?

2.10.oldText: 6. Above all, this rule has no exception (though there are opportunities for exceptions): the idea of political superiority always resolves itself into the idea of psychological superiority, wherever the highest caste is also the priestly caste and, true to its general character, gives itself a title that specifically alludes to its priestly function. In these cases "clean" and "unclean" first confront each other as badges of class distinction, for instance, and here again a "good" and a "bad" develop in a sense that is no longer merely social. Moreover, one should take care not to take these ideas of "clean" and "unclean" too seriously, too broadly, or too symbolically. All the ideas of ancient man must rather be understood, in their early stages, as crude, coarse, physical and narrow to an almost inconceivable extent, and above all as essentially unsymbolical. The "clean man" is originally only a man who washes himself, who abstains from certain foods that lead to skin diseases, who does not sleep with the unclean women of the lower classes, who has a horror of blood — not more, not much more! On the other hand, the very nature of a priestly aristocracy shows why the opposed values should have been sharpened and intensified, so dangerously, at just such an early stage. It is through these opposed values that gulfs are cleft in the social plane which a veritable Achilles of free thought would shudder to cross. Such sacerdotal aristocracies carry a diseased taint from the outset, and so do the habits that prevail in such societies. Averse to action, these habits are a compound of introspection and explosive emotionalism, and out of them comes the introspective morbidity and neurasthenia that cling almost inevitably to all priests at all times. As for the remedy the priests themselves invented for this disease, the philosopher has no option but to say that its effects have proved a hundred times more dangerous than the disease it was supposed to cure. Humanity itself is still sick from the naïvetés of this priestly cure. Take, for instance, certain kinds of diet (abstention from flesh), fasts, sexual continence, flight into the wilderness (a kind of Weir-Mitchell isolation, though of course without that system of excessive feeding and fattening which is the most efficient antidote to all the hysteria of the ascetic ideal). Consider too the whole metaphysic of the priests, with its war on the senses, its enervation, its hair-splitting. Consider its self-hypnotism on the fakir and Brahman principles (it uses Brahman as a glass disc and obsession), and that climax, which we understand only too well, of an unusual satiety with its panacea of nothingness (or God: the demand for a unio mystica with God is the demand of the Buddhist for nothingness, Nirvana — and nothing else!). In sacerdotal societies everything is more dangerous: not merely cures and remedies, but also pride, revenge, cunning, exaltation, love, ambition, virtue, morbidity. Further, one can fairly say that man first becomes an interesting animal on the soil of this essentially dangerous form of human society, the sacerdotal form. In it the human soul has, in a higher sense, gained depth and become evil. And these are the two fundamental ways in which man has shown himself superior to every other animal until now.

2.11.oldText: 7. The reader will already have guessed how easily the priestly mode of valuation can branch off from the knightly aristocratic mode and then grow into its very antithesis. The opposition gets a special impetus whenever the priestly and warrior castes confront each other in mutual jealousy and cannot agree over the prize. The knightly-aristocratic "values" rest on a careful cult of the physical, on a flowering, rich and even effervescing health that goes well beyond what is needed to maintain life, and on war, adventure, the chase, the dance, the tourney — on everything, in fact, that belongs to strong, free and joyous action. The priestly-aristocratic mode of valuation rests, as we have seen, on other hypotheses: war is bad enough for this class! Yet the priests are, as everyone knows, the worst enemies. Why? Because they are the weakest. Their weakness makes their hate swell into a monstrous and sinister shape, the most crafty and most poisonous shape. The really great haters in the history of the world have always been priests, who are also the cleverest haters; set beside the cleverness of priestly revenge, every other cleverness is practically negligible. Human history would be far too fatuous without the cleverness that the weak have brought into it. Take at once the most important instance. Everything the world has done against the "aristocrats," the "mighty," the "masters," the "holders of power," is negligible beside what the Jews have done against those classes. The Jews, that priestly nation, eventually saw that the one way to get satisfaction from its enemies and tyrants was a radical transvaluation of values, which was at the same time an act of the cleverest revenge. Only a nation of priests could use this method, a nation of the most jealously nursed priestly revengefulness. It was the Jews who dared, with terrifying logic, to set against the aristocratic equation (good = aristocratic = beautiful = happy = loved by the gods) the contrary equation, and to hold on to it with the teeth of the most profound hatred (the hatred of weakness): "the wretched alone are the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly alone are the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed, for them alone is salvation. But you, on the other hand, you aristocrats, you men of power, you are to all eternity the evil, the horrible, the covetous, the insatiate, the godless; eternally also shall you be the unblessed, the cursed, the damned!" We know who inherited the fruits of this Jewish transvaluation. Faced with the monstrous and inordinately fateful initiative the Jews took in this most fundamental of all declarations of war, I remember the passage I once wrote (Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 195): that the revolt of the slaves in morals begins, in fact, with the Jews; that this revolt has behind it a history of two millennia, and has now only moved out of our sight because it has achieved victory.

2.14.oldText: 10. The revolt of the slaves in morals begins when resentment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values. This is a resentment felt by creatures who, denied the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge. While every aristocratic morality springs from a triumphant affirmation of its own demands, the slave morality says "no" from the very outset to what is "outside itself," "different from itself," and "not itself": and this "no" is its creative deed. This reversal of the valuing standpoint — this inevitable turn toward the objective instead of back toward the subjective — is typical of "resentment." The slave-morality needs an external and objective world as the condition of its existence; to use physiological terms, it needs objective stimuli in order to be capable of action at all. Its action is fundamentally a reaction. The contrary is the case with the aristocrat's system of values: it acts and grows spontaneously, and seeks its antithesis only in order to say a more grateful and exultant "yes" to itself. Its negative conception, "low," "vulgar," "bad," is merely a pale, late-born foil beside its positive and fundamental conception (saturated as it is with life and passion): "we aristocrats, we good ones, we beautiful ones, we happy ones."

2.16.oldText: 11. This man's method is the exact opposite of the aristocrat's. The aristocrat forms the root idea "good" spontaneously, straight out of himself, and only then, from that material, creates for himself a concept of "bad"! This aristocratic "bad" and that "evil" from the cauldron of unsatisfied hatred are two very different things. The first is an imitation, an "extra," an additional nuance; the second is the original, the beginning, the essential act in the making of a slave-morality. Both "bad" and "evil" have the same opposite, "good," yet how great a difference they mark! For the idea "good" is not the same in each. Ask rather: "Who is really evil, according to the morality of resentment?" The answer, in all sternness, is this: just the good man of the other morality, just the aristocrat, the powerful one, the ruler, but seen through the venomous eye of resentfulness and so given a new color, a new meaning, a new look. We would be the last to deny this. A man who got to know those "good" ones only as enemies learned at the same time not to know them only as "evil enemies." Yet these same men are bound so rigorously inter pares by convention, respect, custom, and gratitude, and still more by mutual vigilance and jealousy inter pares. Among themselves they find so many new ways of showing consideration, self-control, delicacy, loyalty, pride, and friendship. But toward whatever lies outside their circle (where the foreign element, a foreign country, begins) they are not much better than beasts of prey let loose. There they are free of all social control. In the wilderness they can vent, with impunity, the tension built up by being fenced in and shut up within the peace of society. They revert to the innocence of the beast-of-prey conscience, like jubilant monsters who may be coming from a ghastly bout of murder, arson, rape, and torture, with bravado and moral equanimity, as if it were merely some wild student's prank, fully convinced that the poets now have plenty to sing and celebrate. At the core of all these aristocratic races we cannot fail to recognize the beast of prey, the magnificent blond brute, greedily prowling for spoil and victory. This hidden core needed an outlet from time to time; the beast had to get loose again and return to the wilderness. The Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings, all share this need. The aristocratic races left the idea "Barbarian" behind on every path they marched. Nay, a consciousness of this very barbarianism, and even a pride in it, shows itself in their highest civilization (for example, when Pericles tells his Athenians in the celebrated funeral oration, "Our audacity has forced a way over every land and sea, rearing everywhere imperishable memorials of itself for good and for evil"). The audacity of aristocratic races may be mad, absurd, and spasmodic in its expression; their enterprises may be incalculable and fantastic — Pericles sets in special relief and glory the ᾽ραθυμία of the Athenians, their nonchalance and contempt for safety, body, life, and comfort, their awful joy and intense delight in all destruction, in all the ecstasies of victory and cruelty — all these features crystallized, for those who suffered from them, into the picture of the "barbarian," of the "evil enemy," perhaps of the "Goth" and the "Vandal." Even now, the German meets a profound, icy mistrust as soon as he comes to power. That mistrust is still an aftermath of the inextinguishable horror with which Europe, for whole centuries, regarded the wrath of the blond Teuton beast (although there is scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship between the old Germans and ourselves). I once pointed out Hesiod's embarrassment when he conceived the series of social ages and tried to express them in gold, silver, and bronze. The Homeric world confronted him with a contradiction: an age magnificent indeed, but at the same time so awful and so violent. He could resolve it only by making two ages out of one and setting them one behind the other. First came the age of the heroes and demigods, as that world lived on in the memories of the aristocratic families, who found their own ancestors in it. Then came the bronze age, as that same age looked to the descendants of the oppressed, spoiled, ill-treated, exiled, and enslaved: an age of bronze, as I have said, hard, cold, terrible, without feelings and without conscience, crushing everything and spattering everything with blood. Suppose the now-accepted theory is true, that the whole essence of civilization is to train the beast of prey out of man and make of him a tame and civilized animal, a domesticated animal. Then we must undoubtedly regard as the real tools of civilization all those instincts of reaction and resentment, with whose help the aristocratic races, together with their ideals, were finally degraded and overpowered. That is not yet to say that the bearers of those tools also represented civilization. The opposite is not merely probable — nay, it is palpable today. These bearers of vindictive instincts that have to be bottled up, these descendants of all European and non-European slavery, especially of the pre-Aryan population — these people, I say, represent the decline of humanity! These "tools of civilization" are a disgrace to humanity, and in reality they count more as an argument against civilization, more as a reason to be suspicious of it. One may be quite justified in always fearing the blond beast at the core of every aristocratic race, and in staying on one's guard. But who would not a hundred times rather fear, while admiring, than be free of fear and be forever obsessed with the loathsome sight of the distorted, the dwarfed, the stunted, the envenomed? And is that not our fate? What makes us feel repulsion toward "man" today? — for we suffer from "man," there is no doubt about it. It is not fear. It is rather that we have nothing left to fear from men; that the worm "man" is in the foreground and swarms; that the "tame man," the wretched, mediocre, unedifying creature, has learned to consider himself a goal and a pinnacle, an inner meaning, a historic principle, a "higher man." Yes, and he has a certain right to do so, in so far as he feels that, set against that excess of deformity, disease, exhaustion, and effeteness whose odor is beginning to pollute present-day Europe, he at any rate has achieved a relative success; he at any rate still says "yes" to life.

2.33.oldText: 15. In the faith in what? In the love for what? In the hope of what? These weaklings! — they also, forsooth, wish to be the strong some time; there is no doubt about it, some time their kingdom also must come — "the kingdom of God" is their name for it, as has been mentioned: they are so meek in everything! Yet to experience that kingdom one has to live long, to live beyond death — yes, eternal life is necessary, so that one can make up forever for that earthly life "in faith," "in love," "in hope." Make up for what? Make up by what? Dante, it seems to me, made a crass mistake when, with awe-inspiring ingenuity, he placed the inscription "Me too made eternal love" over the gate of his hell. At any rate, the inscription "Me too made eternal hate" would have a much better right to stand over the gate of the Christian Paradise and its "eternal blessedness" — granted, of course, that a truth may rightly stand over the gate to a lie! For what is the blessedness of that Paradise? Possibly we could quickly guess it; but it is better to have it explicitly attested by an authority not to be disparaged in such matters, Thomas of Aquinas, the great teacher and saint. "Beati in regno celesti" he says, as gently as a lamb, "videbunt pœnas damnatorum, ut beatitudo illis magis complaceat." Or if we wish to hear a stronger tone, here is a word from the mouth of a triumphant father of the Church, who warned his disciples against the cruel ecstasies of the public spectacles — But why? Faith offers us much more, he says, de Spectac., c. 29 ss., something much stronger. Thanks to the redemption, joys of quite another kind are at our disposal; instead of athletes we have our martyrs; if we wish for blood, well, we have the blood of Christ — but what then awaits us on the day of his return, of his triumph. And then he goes on, this enraptured visionary: "at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimas et perpetuus judicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta sæculi vetustas et tot ejus nativitates uno igne haurientur. Quæ tunc spectaculi latitudo! Quid admirer! quid rideam! Ubigaudeam! Ubi exultem, spectans tot et tantos reges, qui in cœlum recepti nuntiabantur, cum ipso Jove et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes! Item præsides" (the provincial governors) "persecutores dominici nominis sævioribus quam ipsi flammis sævierunt insultantibus contra Christianos liquescentes! Quos præterea sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras affirmabant! Etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanti nec ad Minois, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes! Tunc magis tragœdi audiendi, magis scilicet vocales" (with louder tones and more violent shrieks) "in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem; tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus rubens, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasiis, sed in igne jaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos velim vivos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum scevierunt. Hic est ille, dicam fabri aut quæstuariæ filius" (as the whole of the following shows, and in particular this well-known description of the mother of Jesus from the Talmud, Tertullian is from here on referring to the Jews), "sabbati destructor, Samarites et dæmonium habens. Hic est quem a Juda redemistis, hic est ille arundine et colaphis diverberatus, sputamentis de decoratus, felle et acete potatus. Hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut resurrexisse dicatur vel hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucæ suæ frequentia commeantium laderentur. Ut talia species, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi prætor aut consul aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate prastabit? Et tamen hæc jam habemus quodammodo per fidem spiritu imaginante repræsentata. Ceterum qualia illa sunt, quæ nec oculus vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt?" (I Cor. ii. 9.) "Credo circo et utraque cavea" (the first and fourth row, or, according to others, the comic and the tragic stage) "et omni studio gratiora." Per fidem: so it stands written.

2.35.oldText: Which of them has been victorious for the time being, Rome or Judæa? There is not a shadow of doubt. Just consider whom you bow down to even in Rome itself today, as though to the quintessence of all the highest values — and not only in Rome, but over almost half the world, wherever man has been tamed or is about to be tamed. You bow to three Jews, as we know, and one Jewess (Jesus of Nazareth, Peter the fisher, Paul the tent-maker, and the mother of the aforesaid Jesus, named Mary). This is very remarkable: Rome is undoubtedly defeated. At any rate, in the Renaissance there was a brilliantly sinister revival of the classical ideal, of the aristocratic valuation of all things. Rome herself, like a man waking from a trance, stirred under the weight of the new Judaized Rome built over her, which looked like an œcumenical synagogue and was called the "Church." But Judæa immediately triumphed again, thanks to that fundamentally popular (German and English) movement of revenge called the Reformation, and thanks also to its inevitable corollary, the restoration of the Church — which also restored the ancient graveyard peace of classical Rome. In the French Revolution Judæa again proved victorious over the classical ideal, in a sense even more crucial and more profound. The last political aristocracy in Europe, that of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century France, broke into pieces under the instincts of a resentful populace. The world had never heard a greater jubilation, a more uproarious enthusiasm. Yet in the midst of it the most monstrous and unexpected thing happened: the ancient ideal itself rose before the eyes and conscience of humanity with all its life and with unheard-of splendor. Against resentment's lying war-cry of the prerogative of the most, against the will to lowliness, abasement, and equalization, the will to a retrogression and twilight of humanity, there rang out once more, stronger, simpler, and more penetrating than ever, the terrible and enchanting counter-warcry of the prerogative of the few! Then, like a final signpost to other ways, Napoleon appeared, the most unique and violent anachronism that ever existed, and in him the incarnate problem of the aristocratic ideal in itself. Consider well what a problem it is: Napoleon, that synthesis of Monster and Superman.

2.36.oldText: 17. Was that the end of it? Was that greatest of all antitheses of ideals thereby put ad acta for all time? Or only postponed, postponed for a long time? May there not come a day when the old conflagration flares up again, far more awful and far more carefully prepared? Further! Should one not wish for that outcome with all one's strength? — will it oneself? demand it oneself? Whoever begins at this point, like my readers, to reflect and think further will find it hard to reach a quick conclusion. That is reason enough for me to conclude myself, taking it for granted that by now it has been sufficiently clear what I mean, exactly what I mean by that dangerous motto inscribed on the body of my last book: Beyond Good and Evil — which at any rate is not the same as "Beyond Good and Bad."

2.39.oldText: On the other hand, it is of course equally necessary to interest physiologists and doctors in these problems (the value of the valuations that have prevailed until now). Here the professional philosophers may be trusted to act as spokesmen and intermediaries, once they have fully managed to turn the relationship between philosophy and physiology and medicine, originally one of coldness and suspicion, into the friendliest and most fruitful reciprocity. In fact, every table of values, every "thou shalt" known to history and ethnology, first needs a physiological elucidation and interpretation, at any rate in preference to a psychological one; all of them equally call for a critique from medical science. The question "What is the value of this or that table of 'values' and morality?" will be asked from the most varied standpoints. The question "valuable for what?", for instance, can never be analyzed with enough nicety. Something that would obviously be valuable for giving a race the greatest possible powers of endurance (or for increasing its adaptability to a specific climate, or for preserving the greatest number) would be nowhere near as valuable if the aim were to develop a stronger species. In gauging values, the good of the majority and the good of the minority are opposed standpoints. We leave it to the naïveté of English biologists to regard the first as intrinsically superior. All the sciences must now pave the way for the future task of the philosopher, understood as this: he must solve the problem of value, he has to fix the hierarchy of values.

3.1.oldText: 2. All this is simply the long history of the origin of responsibility. The task of breeding an animal that can make promises includes, as we have already seen, a more immediate task as its condition and preliminary: first to make man to a certain extent necessitated, uniform, like among his like, regular and therefore calculable. What I have called the "morality of custom" (cp. Dawn of Day, Aphs. 9, 14, and 16) was an immense work: man's actual work on himself during the longest period of the human race, his whole prehistoric work. This work finds its meaning and its great justification (in spite of all its innate hardness, despotism, stupidity and idiocy) in this: with the help of the morality of customs and of social strait-waistcoats, man was made genuinely calculable. But suppose we stand at the end of this colossal process, at the point where the tree finally ripens its fruit and society and its morality of custom at last bring to light what they were only the means to. There we find, as the ripest fruit on its tree, the sovereign individual, who resembles only himself, who has got loose from the morality of custom: the autonomous "super-moral" individual (for "autonomous" and "moral" exclude each other) — in short, the man of the personal, long and independent will, who is able to promise. In him we find a proud consciousness, vibrating in every fibre, of what has at last been achieved and has come alive in him, a genuine consciousness of power and freedom, a feeling of human perfection in general. And this man who has grown to freedom, who is really able to promise, this lord of the free will, this sovereign — how can he fail to know how great his superiority is over everything that cannot bind itself by promises or be its own security, how great a trust, awe and reverence he awakens (he "deserves" all three), and that with this mastery over himself he is necessarily also given mastery over circumstances, over nature, over all creatures with shorter wills and less reliable characters? The "free" man, the owner of a long, unbreakable will, finds in this possession his standard of value. Looking out from himself upon others, he honors or he despises. Just as necessarily as he honors his peers, the strong and the reliable (those who can bind themselves by promises) — that is, everyone who promises like a sovereign, with difficulty, rarely and slowly, who is sparing with his trust but confers honor by the very act of trusting, who gives his word as something that can be relied on because he knows himself strong enough to keep it even in the teeth of disasters, even in the "teeth of fate" — so with equal necessity will he have the heel of his foot ready for the lean and empty jackasses who promise when they have no business to, and his rod of chastisement ready for the liar who already breaks his word at the very moment it is on his lips. The proud knowledge of the extraordinary privilege of responsibility, the consciousness of this rare freedom, of this power over himself and over fate, has sunk right down to his innermost depths and has become an instinct, a dominating instinct. What name will he give to it, to this dominating instinct, if he needs a word for it? There is no doubt about it: the sovereign man calls it his conscience.

3.4.oldText: Have these current genealogists of morals ever allowed themselves even the vaguest notion, for instance, that the cardinal moral idea of "ought" originates in the very material idea of "owe"? Or that punishment developed as a retaliation absolutely independently of any prior assumption about the freedom or determination of the will? — And this to such an extent that a high degree of civilization was always necessary first, before the animal man could begin to make those much more primitive distinctions of "intentional," "negligent," "accidental," "responsible," and their contraries, and apply them in assessing punishment. That idea — "the wrong-doer deserves punishment because he might have acted otherwise" — is nowadays so cheap, obvious, natural and inevitable, and has had to serve as an illustration of how the sentiment of justice appeared on earth; yet in fact it is an exceedingly late, even refined, form of human judgment and inference, and to project it back to the beginning of the world is simply a clumsy violation of the principles of primitive psychology. Throughout the longest period of human history punishment was never based on the evil-doer's responsibility for his action, and was therefore not based on the assumption that only the guilty should be punished. On the contrary, punishment was inflicted for the same reason that parents punish their children even nowadays: out of anger at an injury suffered, an anger that vents itself mechanically on the author of the injury. But this anger is kept in bounds and modified by the idea that every injury has somewhere its equivalent price and can really be paid off, even if by means of pain to the author. Where has this ancient, deep-rooted and now perhaps ineradicable idea, the idea of an equivalence between injury and pain, drawn its strength? I have already revealed its origin: it lies in the contractual relationship between creditor and debtor, which is as old as the existence of legal rights at all, and which in its turn points back to the primary forms of purchase, sale, barter and trade.

3.11.oldText: 9. Measured always by the standard of antiquity (and this antiquity is present, or possible again, in every period), the community stands toward its members in that important and radical relationship of creditor to his "debtors." Man lives in a community and enjoys its advantages (and what advantages! we sometimes underestimate them nowadays). He lives protected and spared, in peace and trust, safe from certain injuries and enmities to which the man outside the community, the "peaceless" man, is exposed (a German understands the original meaning of "Elend" (êlend)). He is safe because he has bound himself by pledges and obligations to the community with regard to those very injuries and enmities. What happens when this is not the case? The community, the defrauded creditor, will get itself paid as well as it can; one can count on that. In this case the direct damage done by the offender is quite secondary. Quite apart from it, the criminal is above all a breaker, a breaker of his word and covenant to the whole, with regard to all the advantages and amenities of communal life in which up to then he had shared. The criminal is a "debtor" who not only fails to repay the advances and advantages given to him, but even sets out to attack his creditor. So in the future he is not only deprived, as is fair, of all these advantages and amenities; he is also reminded how important those advantages were. The wrath of the injured creditor, the community, throws him back into the wild and outlawed state from which he was protected until then. The community repudiates him, and now every kind of enmity can vent itself on him. At this stage of civilization, punishment is simply the copy, the mimicry, of the normal treatment of the hated, despised and conquered enemy, who is deprived not only of every right and protection but of every mercy. So we have the martial law and the triumphant festival of the væ victis! in all its mercilessness and cruelty. This shows why war itself (counting the sacrificial cult of war) has produced all the forms in which punishment has appeared in history.

3.14.oldText: 12. Let me say a little more on the origin and the end of punishment. These are two problems that are, or ought to be, kept separate, but unfortunately they are usually thrown together. And how have our moral genealogists gone about it until now? With their inveterate naïveté. They discover some "end" in punishment, such as revenge or deterrence, and then in all their innocence place this end at the beginning, as the causa fiendi of the punishment, and they have done the trick. But the last use that the "End in Law" should be put to is patching together a history of the origin of law. For any kind of history, perhaps no principle is more pregnant than this one. It is hard to master, yet it should be mastered down to the last detail: the origin of a thing's existence and its final utility, its practical application and its place in a system of ends, are toto cœlo opposed to each other. Whatever exists and prevails anywhere will always be given new purposes by a force superior to it, will be taken over afresh, and will be turned and transformed to new uses. All "happening" in the organic world consists of overpowering and dominating, and all overpowering and domination is a new interpretation and adjustment, which must obscure, or even wholly extinguish, the "meaning" and "end" that existed before. You may understand perfectly the utility of some physiological organ (or of a legal institution, a social custom, a political habit, a form in art or religious worship), and that does not in the least mean you understand its origin. Older men may find this uncomfortable and unpalatable, for people have always believed that to understand the final cause or the utility of a thing, a form, an institution, was to understand why it came into being. By this logic the eye was made to see and the hand was made to grasp, and so punishment too was supposed to have been invented in order to punish. But all ends and all utilities are only signs that a Will to Power has mastered some less powerful force and has stamped on it, out of its own self, the meaning of a function. By the same principle, the whole history of a "Thing," an organ, a custom, can be seen as a continuous "sign-chain" of ever new interpretations and adjustments. Their causes need not be connected with one another at all; sometimes they simply follow and alternate by chance. In the same way, the evolution of a "thing," of a custom, is anything but a progressus toward an end, and even less a logical, direct progressus achieved with the least expense of energy and cost. It is rather a succession of processes of subjugation, more or less profound, more or less independent of one another, that act on the thing. It also includes the resistance offered against each subjugation, the Protean wriggles of defense and reaction, and the results of successful counter-efforts. The form is fluid, but the meaning is more fluid still. Even inside every individual organism it is the same: whenever the whole genuinely grows, the "function" of the single organs shifts. In certain cases the partial perishing of these organs, a reduction in their number (for instance, by the annihilation of the connecting members), can be a symptom of growing strength and perfection. What I mean is this: even partial loss of utility, decay and degeneration, loss of function and purpose, in a word death, belong among the conditions of genuine progressus. Genuine progressus always takes the shape of a will and way to greater power, and is always won at the expense of innumerable smaller powers. A "progress" is measured by the greatness of the sacrifice it demands: humanity as a mass sacrificed to the prosperity of the one stronger species of Man, that would be a progress. I stress this cardinal feature of the historical method all the more because in its essence it runs against the predominant instincts and the prevailing taste. They would much rather put up with absolute casualness, even with the mechanical senselessness of all phenomena, than with the theory of a power-will playing through all phenomena without exception. The democratic idiosyncrasy against everything that rules and wishes to rule, the modern misarchism (to coin a bad word for a bad thing), has gradually dressed itself so thoroughly in the guise of intellectualism, the most abstract intellectualism, that today it penetrates step by step, and has the right to penetrate, even the most exact and apparently most objective sciences. In my view it has already come to dominate the whole of physiology and biology, to their detriment, as is obvious, because it has spirited away a radical idea, the idea of true activity. Under the tyranny of this idiosyncrasy the theory of "adaptation" is pushed to the front of the argument and exploited. Adaptation means a second-class activity, a mere capacity for "reacting"; in fact, life itself has been defined (by Herbert Spencer) as an ever more effective internal adaptation to external circumstances. This definition, however, fails to grasp the real essence of life, its will to power. It fails to see the paramount superiority of those plastic forces of spontaneity, aggression and encroachment, with their new interpretations and tendencies, for which adaptation is only a natural corollary. As a result, the sovereign office of the highest functionaries in the organism itself (among which the life-will appears as an active and formative principle) is repudiated. One remembers Huxley's reproach to Spencer of his "administrative Nihilism": but it is a case of something much more than "administration."

3.29.oldText: 24. I conclude with three queries, as you will see. "Is an ideal actually set up here, or is one pulled down?" I am perhaps asked.... But have you asked yourselves sufficiently how dear a payment the setting up of every ideal in the world has exacted? To achieve that, how much truth must always be slandered and misunderstood, how many lies must be sanctified, how much conscience must be disturbed, how many pounds of "God" must be sacrificed every time? For a sanctuary to be set up, a sanctuary has got to be destroyed: that is a law. Show me an instance where it has not been fulfilled!... We modern men inherit the immemorial tradition of vivisecting the conscience and practicing cruelty on our animal selves. That is the sphere of our most protracted training, perhaps of our artistic prowess, at any rate of our dilettantism and our perverted taste. Man has for too long regarded his natural proclivities with an "evil eye," so that eventually they have become affiliated in his system to a bad conscience. The converse endeavor would in itself be feasible, but who is strong enough to attempt it? It would be to affiliate to the "bad conscience" all those unnatural proclivities, all those transcendental aspirations contrary to sense, instinct, nature and animalism: in short, all past and present ideals, which are all ideals opposed to life and slandering the world. To whom is one to turn nowadays with such hopes and pretensions? It is just the good men that we should thus bring down about our ears. And in addition, as stands to reason, the indolent, the hedgers, the vain, the hysterical, the tired.... What is more offensive, or more thoroughly calculated to alienate, than giving any hint of the exalted severity with which we treat ourselves? And again, how conciliatory and full of love the whole world shows itself towards us as soon as we do as all the world does, and "let ourselves go" like all the world. For such an achievement we need spirits of a different caliber from what seems really feasible in this age: spirits made potent through wars and victories, to whom conquest, adventure, danger, even pain, have become a need. For it we need to be used to sharp, rare air, to winter wanderings, to ice and mountains literal and metaphorical. We even need a kind of sublime malice, a supreme and most self-conscious insolence of knowledge, which is the appanage of great health. We need (to sum up the awful truth) just this great health!

4.3.oldText: 2. What do ascetic ideals mean? Or, to take one case on which I have often been consulted: what does it mean when an artist like Richard Wagner pays homage to chastity in his old age? In a certain sense he had always done so, of course. But only at the very end did he do it in an ascetic sense. What does this "change of attitude" mean, this radical revolution (for that is what it was)? Wagner swung right round into his own opposite. And what does it mean when an artist swings round into his own opposite? Here, if we are willing to dwell a little on the question, we think at once of the best, strongest, gayest and boldest period that Wagner's life perhaps ever had. It was the time when he was deeply and genuinely absorbed in the idea of "Luther's Wedding." Who knows by what chance we now have the Meistersingers in place of that wedding music? And how much of the one may be an echo of the other? Still, there is no doubt that the theme would have praised chastity. It would certainly have praised sensuality as well; and even so it would have seemed quite in order, and just as Wagnerian. For chastity and sensuality are not necessarily opposed: every good marriage, every authentic, heart-felt love, rises above that opposition. It seems to me that Wagner would have done well to bring this pleasing reality home to his Germans once more, with a bold and graceful "Luther Comedy." There were and are many revilers of sensuality among the Germans, and perhaps Luther's greatest merit is just that he had the courage of his sensuality (it used to be called, prettily enough, "evangelistic freedom "). Even where the opposition between chastity and sensuality really does exist, fortunately it has not needed to be a tragic one for some time now. That should hold for all beings sound in mind and body. They are far from counting their delicate balance between "animal" and "angel" as, on the face of it, one of the principles opposed to existence. The most subtle and brilliant spirits, Goethe and Hafiz for example, have even found in it a further charm of life. Such "conflicts" actually tempt one to live. On the other hand, it is only too clear what happens when these ruined swine are reduced to worshipping chastity (and there are such swine): all they see and worship in it is the opposite of themselves, the opposite of ruined swine. Oh, what tragic grunting and eagerness! Just imagine it. They worship that painful and superfluous contrast which Richard Wagner in his last years undoubtedly wanted to set to music and put on the stage! "For what purpose, forsooth?" we may fairly ask. What did the swine matter to him; what do they matter to us?

4.6.oldText: 5. What, then, do ascetic ideals mean? In the case of an artist we are beginning to see: nothing at all ... or so much that it is as good as nothing at all. Indeed, what use are they? For a long time our artists have not taken a position independent enough, in the world or against it, to make their valuations, or any changes in them, interesting. At all times they have been the valets of some morality, philosophy or religion. Unfortunately they have also often been the inordinately supple courtiers of their clients and patrons, and the inquisitive toadies of the powers that be, or even of the powers still to come. At the very least, they always need a rampart, a support, some authority already in place. Artists never stand by themselves; standing alone goes against their deepest instincts. Thus Richard Wagner, "when the time had come," took the philosopher Schopenhauer as his covering man in front, as his rampart. Who would think it even possible that he could have had the courage for an ascetic ideal without the support of Schopenhauer's philosophy, without the authority of Schopenhauer, which dominated Europe in the seventies? (Here I set aside the question whether an artist without the milk of an orthodoxy could have existed at all.) This brings us to the more serious question: what does it mean when a real philosopher pays homage to the ascetic ideal? I mean a really self-dependent intellect like Schopenhauer, a man and knight with a glance of bronze, who has the courage to be himself, who knows how to stand alone without first waiting for men to cover him in front and for nods from his superiors. Let us look at once at Schopenhauer's remarkable attitude to art, an attitude that even fascinates certain types. For that, obviously, is why Richard Wagner suddenly went over to Schopenhauer (persuaded to it, as is well known, by a poet, Herwegh). He went over so completely that a rift opened, a total theoretical contradiction, between his earlier and his later æsthetic faiths. The earlier was set out, for example, in Opera and Drama; the later in the writings he published from 1870 onwards. Above all, from then on Wagner had no scruples about changing his judgment of the value and position of music itself (and this volte-face is what alienates us most). Until then he had made music a means, a medium, a "woman," who needed an end in order to thrive, a man, that is, the drama. What did he care? He suddenly saw that the novelty of the Schopenhauerian theory could achieve more in majorem musicæ gloriam, that is, through the sovereignty of music as Schopenhauer understood it. Music was abstracted from all the other arts and set against them, as the independent art-in-itself. It did not reflect the phenomenal world as the other arts do. It was rather the language of the will itself, speaking straight out of the "abyss" as the will's most personal, original and direct manifestation. This extraordinary rise in the value of music (a rise that seemed to grow out of the Schopenhauerian philosophy) came at once with an unprecedented rise in the esteem given to the musician himself. Now he became an oracle, a priest, nay, more than a priest: a kind of mouthpiece for the "intrinsic essence of things," a telephone from the other world. From then on he spoke not only music, this ventriloquist of God; he spoke metaphysic. Is it any wonder that one day he spoke ascetic ideals?

4.10.oldText: 9. A certain asceticism, a grimly gay and wholehearted renunciation, is, as we have seen, among the most favorable conditions for the highest intellectualism, and so also for its most natural consequences. It should therefore not surprise us that philosophers in particular have always had a certain fondness for the ascetic ideal. A serious historical investigation shows that the bond between the ascetic ideal and philosophy is tighter and stronger still. One may say that philosophy learned to take its first steps and baby paces only in the leading strings of this ideal — alas, how clumsy, alas, how cross, alas, how ready to tumble and lie on its belly was this shy little darling of a brat on its bandy legs! The early history of philosophy is like that of all good things: for a long time they lacked the courage to be themselves, kept looking around to see whether anyone would come to help them, and were afraid of everyone who looked at them. Just list the particular tendencies and virtues of the philosopher in order: his tendency to doubt, to deny, to wait (to be "ephectic"), to analyze, search, explore and dare, to compare and to equalize; his will to be neutral and objective, his will for everything that is "sine ira et studio". Has anyone yet realized that for quite a long period these tendencies ran against the first claims of morality and conscience? (To say nothing of Reason, which even Luther chose to call Frau Klüglin, the sly whore.) Has anyone yet appreciated that a philosopher who arrives at self-consciousness must feel himself an incarnate "nitimur in vetitum" — and must therefore guard himself against "his own sensations," against self-consciousness? I repeat: it is the same with all the good things we now pride ourselves on. Judged even by the standard of the ancient Greeks, our whole modern life, in so far as it is not weakness but power and the consciousness of power, looks like pure "Hybris" and godlessness. For the very opposites of the things we honor today had conscience on their side for a long time, and God as their guardian. "Hybris" is our whole attitude to nature nowadays, our violation of nature with the aid of machinery and the unscrupulous ingenuity of our scientists and engineers. "Hybris" is our attitude to God — that is, to some alleged teleological and ethical spider behind the meshes of the great trap of the causal web. Like Charles the Bold in his war with Louis the Eleventh, we may say, "je combats l'universelle araignée." "Hybris" is our attitude to ourselves, for we experiment on ourselves in a way we would not permit with any animal, and gladly and curiously we cut open our soul while the body lives. What does the "salvation" of the soul matter to us now? Afterwards we heal ourselves; being ill is instructive, we do not doubt it, even more instructive than being well — inoculators of disease seem to us today even more necessary than any medicine-men and "saviors." There is no doubt that we do violence to ourselves nowadays, we crackers of the soul's kernel, we incarnate riddles who are forever asking riddles, as though life were nothing but the cracking of a nut. And precisely by this we must become, day by day, more and more worthy to be questioned and to question. Perhaps by this we also become worthier to — live?

4.15.oldText: 11. And now that we have caught sight of the ascetic priest, let us take up our problem. What is the meaning of the ascetic ideal? Now it first becomes serious — vitally serious. We now face the real representatives of seriousness. "What is the meaning of all seriousness?" This still more radical question is perhaps already on the tip of our tongue: a question, fairly, for physiologists, which we skip for now. In that ideal the ascetic priest finds not only his faith but also his will, his power, his interest. His right to exist stands or falls with that ideal. No wonder that we run into a terrible opponent here (supposing, of course, that we are opponents of that ideal) — an opponent fighting for his life against those who repudiate it!... On the other hand, it is improbable from the start that so biased an attitude toward our problem will do him much good. The ascetic priest will hardly prove the happiest champion of his own ideal (on the same principle by which a woman usually fails when she wants to champion "woman"), still less the most objective critic and judge of the controversy we have raised. So much is already clear: we shall have to help him defend himself properly against us, rather than fear being too well beaten by him. The idea in dispute is the value our life has from the standpoint of the ascetic priests. They set this life (together with the whole of which it is a part, "Nature," "the world," the whole sphere of becoming and passing away) in relation to an existence of quite another kind, which it excludes and to which it is opposed, unless it denies itself. In that case, the case of an ascetic life, life is taken as a bridge to that other existence. The ascetic treats life as a maze in which one must walk backwards until one reaches the place where it starts; or he treats it as an error which one may, nay must, refute by action, for he demands that he be followed and enforces his valuation of existence wherever he can. What does this mean? Such a monstrous valuation is no exceptional case or curiosity in human history; it is one of the most general and persistent facts there are. Someone who read the capital letters of our earthly life from the vantage of a distant star might perhaps conclude that the earth was the especially ascetic planet, a den of discontented, arrogant and repulsive creatures who never got rid of a deep disgust with themselves, with the world, with all life, and who hurt themselves as much as possible out of pleasure in hurting — presumably their one and only pleasure. Consider how regularly, how universally, how practically at every period the ascetic priest appears: he belongs to no particular race; he thrives everywhere; he comes out of all classes. It is not that he perhaps bred this valuation by heredity and propagated it — the contrary is the case. A necessity of the first order must be what makes this species, hostile as it is to life, grow again and thrive again. Life itself must certainly have an interest in the continuance of such a type of self-contradiction. For an ascetic life is a self-contradiction. Here rules a resentment without parallel, the resentment of an insatiate instinct and ambition that wants to be master, not over some element in life, but over life itself, over its deepest, strongest, innermost conditions. Here an attempt is made to use power to dam the sources of power. Here the green eye of jealousy turns even against physiological well-being, especially against its expression, beauty and joy; while pleasure is felt and sought in abortion, decay, pain, misfortune, ugliness, voluntary punishment, in the exercising, flagellation and sacrifice of the self. All this is in the highest degree paradoxical: we face a rift that wills itself to be a rift, that enjoys itself in this very suffering and grows more and more certain of itself, more and more triumphant, in proportion as its own presupposition, physiological vitality, declines. "The triumph just in the supreme agony": under this extravagant emblem the ascetic ideal has fought from of old. In this mystery of seduction, in this picture of rapture and torture, it recognized its brightest light, its salvation, its final victory. Crux, nux, lux — it has all three in one.

4.17.oldText: 13. But let us turn back. The self-contradiction that seems to show itself among the ascetics, "Life turned against Life," is simply nonsense — this much is absolutely obvious — when judged from the physiological standpoint and not, now, the psychological one. It can only be an apparent contradiction. It has to be a kind of provisional expression, an explanation, a formula, an adjustment: a psychological misunderstanding of something whose real nature could not be grasped for a long time, and whose real essence could not be described. It is a mere word jammed into an old gap in human knowledge. Put briefly, the facts that count against its being real are these. The ascetic ideal comes out of the protective, self-preserving instincts of a decadent life, a life that tries by every means it has to hold its position and fight for its existence. It points to a partial physiological depression and exhaustion, and the deepest, still intact life-instincts keep fighting this ceaselessly with new weapons and new discoveries. The ascetic ideal is one such weapon. So its position is exactly the reverse of what its worshippers imagine: life is struggling in it and through it with death and against death, and the ascetic ideal is a dodge to keep life going. History teaches something important about how far this ideal could rule over man and exercise power over him, especially in every place where the civilization and taming of man was completed. What it shows is the diseased state of man up to now, at any rate of the tamed man: his physiological struggle with death (more precisely, with disgust with life, with exhaustion, with the wish for the "end"). The ascetic priest is the incarnate wish for an existence of another kind, on another plane. He is, in fact, the highest point of this wish, its official ecstasy and passion. Yet the very strength of this wish is the fetter that ties him down here. It is just this that turns him into a tool, one who has to labor to create more favorable conditions for earthly existence, for existence on the human plane. With this very strength he holds the whole herd of failures, distortions, abortions, unfortunates and sufferers from themselves of every kind fast to existence, while he walks instinctively ahead of them as their herdsman. You understand me already: this ascetic priest, this apparent enemy of life, this denier — he actually belongs among the really great conservative and affirmative forces of life.... Where does this diseased state come from? For man is more diseased, more uncertain, more changeable and more unstable than any other animal, there is no doubt of it — he is the diseased animal. So where does it spring from? Certainly he has also dared more, innovated more, braved more and challenged fate more than all the other animals put together. He is the great experimenter with himself, the unsatisfied, the insatiate, who fights for supreme mastery against beast, Nature and gods. He is the as yet ever uncompelled, the ever future, who can no longer find any rest from his own aggressive strength, driven mercilessly on by the spur of the future dug into the flesh of the present. How could so brave and rich an animal fail to be also the most endangered, the animal with the longest and deepest sickness among all sick animals?... Man grows sick of it, and often enough whole epidemics of this satiety break out (as around 1348, the time of the Dance of Death). Yet even this very nausea, this tiredness, this disgust with himself, is thrown off by him with such force that it is at once made into a new fetter. His "nay" to life brings forth, as though by magic, an abundance of graceful "yeas"; and even when he wounds himself, this master of destruction and of self-destruction, it is the wound itself afterward that forces him to live.

4.18.oldText: 14. The more normal this sickliness in man is — and we cannot deny that it is normal — the more honor is owed to the rare cases of psychical and physical powerfulness, the windfalls of humanity, and the more strictly the sound must be protected from that worst of airs, the air of the sick-room. Is that being done? The sick are the greatest danger to the healthy; the strong are harmed not by the strongest but by the weakest. Is that known? Looked at broadly, it is not the fear of man that we should wish to see diminished, not for a minute. This fear forces the strong to be strong and at times terrible, and so keeps the sound type of man intact. What we must fear, what works with a fatality found in no other fate, is not the great fear of man but the great nausea with man, and equally the great pity for man. Suppose these two were one day to be joined in marriage. The maximum of monstrousness would inevitably come into the world at once: the "last will" of man, his will for nothingness, Nihilism. And indeed the road to it is well paved. Anyone who has not only a nose to smell with but also eyes and ears will sniff, almost wherever he goes today, an air something like that of a mad-house or a hospital. I am speaking, as stands to reason, of the cultured areas of mankind, of every kind of "Europe" that there is in fact in the world. The sick are the great danger to man, not the evil, not the "beasts of prey." The ones who are botched, oppressed and broken from the start, the weakest, are the ones who most undermine life under the feet of man, and who instil the most dangerous venom and skepticism into our trust in life, in man, in ourselves. Where shall we escape it, that covert look (which leaves us carrying away a deep sadness), that averted look of the man who was misborn from the beginning, the look that betrays what such a man says to himself — the look that is a groan? "Would that I were something else," this look groans, "but there is no hope. I am what I am: how could I get away from myself? And, verily — I am sick of myself!" Out of such a soil of self-contempt, a veritable swamp soil, grows that weed, that poisonous growth, so tiny, so hidden, so ignoble, so sugary. Here the worms of revenge and vindictiveness swarm; here the air reeks of things secret and unmentionable; here the net of the most malignant conspiracy is forever being spun — the conspiracy of the sufferers against the sound and the victorious; here the sight of the victorious is hated. And what lying, so as never to admit this hate as hate! What a show of big words and attitudes, what an art of "righteous" calumniation! These abortions! What noble eloquence pours from their lips! What a quantity of sugary, slimy, humble submission oozes in their eyes! What do they really want? At any rate to represent righteousness, love, wisdom, superiority: that is the ambition of these "lowest ones," these sick ones! And how clever such an ambition makes them! In fact you cannot help admiring the counterfeiter's skill with which the stamp of virtue, even the ring, the golden ring of virtue, is copied here. They have taken out a lease on virtue absolutely for themselves, these weaklings and wretched invalids, there is no doubt of it. "We alone are the good, the righteous," they say, "we alone are the homines bonæ voluntatis." They stalk about among us as living reproaches, as warnings to us — as though health, fitness, strength, pride, the sensation of power were vicious things in themselves, for which one would someday have to do penance, bitter penance. Oh, how ready they themselves are in their hearts to make others do penance, how they thirst to be hangmen!

4.19.oldText: Among them are plenty of revengeful ones disguised as judges, who forever mouth the word righteousness like a venomous spittle — with mouth, I say, always pursed, always ready to spit at anything that does not wear a discontented look but goes its way in good cheer. Among them, too, is that most loathsome species of the vain, the lying abortions, who make a point of playing "beautiful souls," and perhaps bring to market, as "purity of heart," their distorted sensualism wrapped up in verses and other bandages: the species of "self-comforters" and masturbators of their own souls. The sick man wants to represent some form of superiority, and has an instinct for crooked paths leading to a tyranny over the healthy — where can this will to power of the very weakest not be found? The sick woman especially: no one surpasses her in refinements of ruling, oppressing, tyrannizing. The sick woman, moreover, spares nothing living and nothing dead; she digs up again the most deeply buried things (the Bogos say, "Woman is a hyena"). Look into the background of every family, every body, every community: everywhere you will find the fight of the sick against the healthy. It is mostly a silent fight, waged with minute poisoned powders, with pin-pricks, with spiteful grimaces of patience, but at times also with that diseased pharisaism of pure pantomime which likes best to play the role of "righteous indignation." It can make itself heard right into the hallowed chambers of knowledge, this hoarse yelping of sick hounds, this rabid lying and frenzy of such "noble" Pharisees (I remind readers who have ears once more of that Berlin apostle of revenge, Eugen Dühring, who makes the most disreputable and revolting use of moral refuse anywhere in present-day Germany; Dühring, the paramount moral blusterer there is today, even among his own kidney, the Anti-Semites). They are all men of resentment, these physiological distortions and worm-riddled objects, a whole quivering kingdom of burrowing revenge, indefatigable and insatiable in its outbursts against the happy, and equally so in its disguises for revenge, its pretexts for revenge. When will they really reach their final, fondest, most sublime triumph of revenge? Doubtless when they succeed in pushing their own misery, in fact all misery, into the consciousness of the happy, so that the happy begin one day to be ashamed of their happiness and perhaps say to themselves when they meet, "It is a shame to be happy! there is too much misery!" ... But there could not possibly be a greater and more fatal misunderstanding than for the happy, the fit, the strong in body and soul to begin in this way to doubt their right to happiness. Away with this "perverse world"! Away with this shameful soddenness of sentiment! To stop the sick from making the healthy sick — for that is what such soddenness comes to — ought to be our supreme object in the world. For this it is above all essential that the healthy stay separated from the sick, that they even guard themselves from the look of the sick, that they not even associate with the sick. Or is it perhaps their mission to be nurses or doctors? They could not mistake and disown their mission more grossly. The higher must not degrade itself into the tool of the lower, and the pathos of distance must keep their missions separate to all eternity. The right of the happy to exist, the right of bells with a full tone over the discordant cracked bells, is verily a thousand times greater: they alone are the sureties of the future, they alone are bound to man's future. What they can do and must do, the sick can never do and should never do! But if they are to be enabled to do what only they must do, how can they possibly be free to play the doctor, the comforter, the "Saviour" of the sick?... And therefore good air! good air! and away, at any rate, from the neighborhood of all the madhouses and hospitals of civilization! And therefore good company, our own company, or solitude if it must be so! But away, at any rate, from the evil fumes of internal corruption and the secret worm-eaten state of the sick! So that, indeed, my friends, we may defend ourselves, at least for a while longer, against the two worst plagues that could have been kept in store for us — against the great nausea with man! against the great pity for man!

4.20.oldText: 15. Suppose you have understood in all their depths why it cannot be the business of the healthy to nurse the sick and make them healthy — and I demand that you grasp these reasons profoundly and understand them profoundly. Then it follows that you have grasped a further necessity: the necessity of doctors and nurses who are themselves sick. And now we have and hold, with both hands, the essence of the ascetic priest. We have to accept him as the predestined savior, herdsman and champion of the sick herd; only then do we first understand his awful historic mission. His kingdom is lordship over sufferers; his instinct points him toward it, and in it he finds his own special art, his master-skill, his kind of happiness.
