He must himself be sick, he must be kith and kin to the sick and the abortions, so as to understand them and come to an understanding with them. But he must also be strong, even more master of himself than of others, impregnable, indeed, in his will for power, so that he can win the trust and the awe of the weak and be their hold, bulwark, prop, compulsion, overseer, tyrant, god. He has to protect them, protect his herds — against whom? Against the healthy, doubtless, and also against envy of the healthy. He must be the natural adversary and scorner of every rough, stormy, unbridled, hard, violently predatory health and power. The priest is the first form of the more delicate animal, which scorns more easily than it hates. He will not be spared a war with the beasts of prey, a war of guile (of "spirit") rather than of force, as is self-evident. In certain cases he will find it necessary to conjure up out of himself, or at any rate to represent in practice, a new type of the beast of prey — a new animal monstrosity in which the polar bear, the supple, cold, crouching panther and, not least important, the fox are joined together in a trinity as fascinating as it is fearsome. If necessity demands it, he will step onto the scene with bearish seriousness, venerable, wise, cold, full of treacherous superiority, as the herald and mouthpiece of mysterious powers. Sometimes he will go even among the other kind of beasts of prey, determined to sow suffering, discord and self-contradiction on their soil wherever he can, and only too sure of his art of being, at all times, lord of sufferers. He brings with him, doubtless, salve and balsam; but before he can play the physician he must first wound. So while he soothes the pain the wound makes, he at the same time poisons the wound. He is well versed in this above all, this wizard and wild beast tamer, in whose presence everything healthy must needs fall ill and everything ill must needs grow tame. He protects his sick herd well enough, indeed, this strange herdsman. He also protects them against themselves, against the sparks of wickedness, knavery, malice and all the other ills that the plaguey and the sick are heir to (sparks that fly even in the center of the herd). With cunning, hardness and stealth he fights anarchy and the ever imminent break-up inside the herd, where resentment, that most dangerous blasting-stuff and explosive, accumulates and accumulates. His real feat, his supreme usefulness, is to get rid of this blasting-stuff in such a way that it does not blow up the herd and the herdsman. If you want the value of the priestly life in the shortest formula, it would be correct to say that the priest is the diverter of the course of resentment. For every sufferer instinctively looks for a cause of his suffering; to put it more exactly, for a doer — to put it still more precisely, for a sentient responsible doer — in brief, for something living on which he can vent his emotions, actually or in effigie, on any pretext. For the venting of emotions is the sufferer's greatest attempt at alleviation, that is to say, at stupefaction: his mechanically desired narcotic against pain of any kind. In this phenomenon alone, according to my judgment, lies the real physiological cause of resentment, revenge and their family — that is, in a demand for the deadening of pain through emotion. This cause is generally sought, but in my view very erroneously, in the defensive parry of a bare protective principle of reaction, of a "reflex movement" at any sudden hurt and danger, just as a decapitated frog still moves in order to get away from a corrosive acid. But the difference is fundamental. In one case the aim is to prevent being hurt any further; in the other the aim is to deaden a racking, insidious, nearly unbearable pain with a more violent emotion of any kind whatsoever, and at any rate for the time being to drive it out of the consciousness. For this an emotion is needed, as wild an emotion as possible, and to excite that emotion some excuse or other is needed. "It must be somebody's fault that I feel bad" — this kind of reasoning is peculiar to all invalids, and the more pronounced the more ignorant they remain of the real cause of their feeling bad, the physiological cause (the cause may lie in a disease of the nervus sympathicus, or in an excessive secretion of bile, or in a lack of sulphate and phosphate of potash in the blood, or in pressure in the bowels that stops the circulation of the blood, or in degeneration of the ovaries, and so forth). All sufferers are awfully resourceful and ingenious at finding excuses for painful emotions. They even enjoy their jealousy and their broodings over base actions and apparent injuries. They burrow through the intestines of their past and present in search of obscure mysteries, where they are free to wallow in a torturing suspicion and get drunk on the venom of their own malice. They tear open the oldest wounds, they make themselves bleed from scars long since healed, and they turn friend, wife, child and everything nearest to them into evil-doers. "I suffer: it must be somebody's fault" — so thinks every sick sheep. But his herdsman, the ascetic priest, tells him, "Quite so, my sheep, it must be the fault of someone; but you yourself are that someone, it is all the fault of yourself alone — it is the fault of yourself alone against yourself." That is bold enough, false enough, but one thing at least is achieved; thereby, as I have said, the course of resentment is — diverted.

4.23.oldText: 17. But is he really a physician, this ascetic priest? We already understand why we are scarcely allowed to call him one, however much he likes to feel like a "saviour" and to be worshipped as one. He combats only the actual suffering, the sufferer's discomfort, not its cause, not the actual state of sickness. This must be our most radical objection to priestly medication. Yet put yourself just once into that point of view, which the priests have a monopoly on, and you will find it hard to exhaust your amazement at all he has seen, sought and found from that standpoint. The mitigation of suffering, every kind of "consoling" — all this shows itself as his very genius. With what ingenuity has he interpreted his mission as consoler, with what aplomb and audacity has he chosen the weapons the part requires! Christianity in particular should be called a great treasure-chamber of ingenious consolations, so great a store of refreshing, soothing, deadening drugs has it piled up within itself. It has hazarded so many of the most dangerous and daring expedients; with such subtlety and refinement, Oriental refinement, it has divined which emotional stimulants can conquer, at least for a time, the deep depression, the leaden fatigue and the black melancholy of physiological cripples. For, speaking generally, all religions are mainly concerned with fighting a certain fatigue and heaviness that has infected everything. You can take it as prima facie probable that in certain places in the world there was almost bound to prevail from time to time, among large masses of the population, a sense of physiological depression. Owing to their lack of physiological knowledge, this did not appear to their consciousness as such, and so its "cause" and its cure could only be sought and tried in the science of moral psychology (this, in fact, is my most general formula for what is generally called a "religion"). Such a feeling of depression can have the most diverse origins. It may result from the crossing of too heterogeneous races (or of classes — genealogical and racial differences also show themselves in the classes: the European "Weltschmerz," the "Pessimism" of the nineteenth century, is really the result of an absurd and sudden class-mixture). It may be brought about by a mistaken emigration, a race falling into a climate for which its power of adaptation is insufficient (the case of the Indians in India). It may be the effect of old age and fatigue (the Parisian pessimism from 1850 onwards). It may come from a wrong diet (the alcoholism of the Middle Ages, the nonsense of vegetarianism — though these have in their favor the authority of Sir Christopher in Shakespeare). It may come from blood-deterioration, malaria, syphilis and the like (German depression after the Thirty Years' War, which infected half of Germany with evil diseases and thereby paved the way for German servility, for German pusillanimity). In such a case a war on a grand scale against the feeling of depression is invariably attempted. Let us inform ourselves briefly about its most important practices and phases (I leave aside, as stands to reason, the actual philosophic war against the feeling of depression, which is usually simultaneous — it is interesting enough, but too absurd, too practically negligible, too full of cobwebs, too much of a hole-and-corner affair, especially when pain is proved to be a mistake, on the naïf hypothesis that pain must needs vanish once the mistake underlying it is recognized — but behold! it does anything but vanish ...). That dominant depression is fought primarily by weapons that reduce the consciousness of life itself to the lowest degree. Wherever possible, no more wishes, no more wants; avoid everything that produces emotion, that produces "blood" (eating no salt, the fakir hygiene); no love; no hate; equanimity; no revenge; no getting rich; no work; begging; as far as possible, no woman, or as little woman as possible; as far as the intellect is concerned, Pascal's principle, "il faut s'abêtir." In ethical and psychological language, the result is "self-annihilation," "sanctification"; in physiological language, "hypnotism." It is the attempt to find some approximate human equivalent for what hibernation is for certain animals and æstivation for many tropical plants: a minimum of assimilation and metabolism in which life just manages to subsist without really entering the consciousness. An amazing amount of human energy has been devoted to this object — perhaps uselessly? There cannot be the slightest doubt that these sportsmen of "saintliness," of whom nearly every nation has at times had an abundance, really found a genuine relief from what they fought with such rigorous training. In countless cases they really did escape deep physiological depression with the help of their system of hypnotism, and their method is consequently counted among the most universal ethnological facts. Similarly it is improper to treat such a plan of starving the physical element and the desires as itself a symptom of insanity (as a clumsy species of roast-beef-eating "freethinkers" and Sir Christophers are fain to do). All the more certain is it that their method can and does pave the way to all kinds of mental disturbances, for instance "inner lights" (as with the Hesychasts of Mount Athos), auditory and visual hallucinations, voluptuous ecstasies and effervescences of sensualism (the history of St. Theresa). The explanation the victims give of such events is always the acme of fanatical falsehood; this is self-evident. Note well, however, the tone of implicit gratitude that rings in the very will to an explanation of such a character. They always regard the supreme state, salvation itself, that final goal of universal hypnosis and peace, as the mystery of mysteries, which even the most supreme symbols are inadequate to express. They regard it as an entry and homecoming to the essence of things, a liberation from all illusions, "knowledge," "truth," "being," an escape from every end, every wish, every action, something even beyond Good and Evil.

4.28.oldText: 19. We have already come to know the ascetic priest's methods: stifling all vitality, mechanical activity, the little joy, and above all the "love your neighbour" herd organization, which awakens the communal consciousness of power to such a pitch that the individual's disgust with himself is eclipsed by his delight in the community's thriving. By modern standards these are the "innocent" methods of fighting depression. Let us turn now to the more interesting subject of the "guilty" methods. They all come down to one thing: producing emotional excess, which serves as the most effective anæsthetic against the depressing state of protracted pain. That is why priestly ingenuity has proved quite inexhaustible in working out one question: "By what means can you produce an emotional excess?" This sounds harsh. Obviously it would sound nicer, and grate less on the ear, if I said instead, if you please: "The ascetic priest always made use of the enthusiasm that lies in all strong emotions." But why go on soothing the delicate ears of our modern effeminates? Why should we budge a single inch before their verbal Pecksniffianism? For us psychologists that would be practical Pecksniffianism in its own right, quite apart from the nausea it gives us. Nowadays a psychologist's good taste (others might say his righteousness) lies, if anywhere, in fighting the shamefully moralized language that smears every modern judgment on men and things. For do not deceive yourself: the chief mark of modern souls and modern books is not lying, but the innocence that comes with their intellectual dishonesty. Meeting this "innocence" everywhere is the most distasteful part of the rather dangerous business a modern psychologist has to take on. It is part of our great danger; it is a road that perhaps leads us straight to the great nausea. I know quite well what all modern books will serve for, and can serve for (granted that they last, which I do not fear, and granted equally that some day there will be a generation with a more rigid, more severe and healthier taste). I know what all modernity will serve for in the eyes of posterity: as an emetic, — and this by reason of its moral sugariness and falsity, its ingrained feminism, which it is pleased to call "Idealism," and at any rate believes to be idealism. Our cultured men of today, our "good" men, do not lie — that is true; but it does them no honor! The real lie, the genuine, determined, "honest" lie (on whose value you can listen to Plato), would be far too tough and strong for them. It would require them to do what people have been forbidden to ask of them: to open their eyes to their own selves, and to learn to tell "true" from "false" in their own selves. Only the dishonest lie suits them. Whatever feels itself a good man can take no other attitude to anything than that of a dishonorable liar, an absolute liar, but none the less an innocent liar, a blue-eyed liar, a virtuous liar. These "good men" are all now tainted with morality through and through, and as far as honor goes they are disgraced and corrupted for all eternity. Which of them could stand one further truth "about man"? Or, to put it more tangibly, which of them could put up with a true biography? Take a few instances. Lord Byron wrote a most personal autobiography, but Thomas Moore was "too good" for it and burned his friend's papers. Dr. Gwinner, Schopenhauer's executor, is said to have done the same; for Schopenhauer also wrote much about himself, and perhaps also against himself: (εἰς ἑαντόν). The virtuous American Thayer, Beethoven's biographer, suddenly broke off his work: he had reached a certain point in that honorable and simple life and could stand it no longer. Moral: What sensible man nowadays writes one honest word about himself? He must already belong to the Order of Holy Foolhardiness. We are promised an autobiography of Richard Wagner; who doubts that it would be a clever autobiography? Think, if you please, of the grotesque horror the Catholic priest Janssen aroused in Germany with his inconceivably square and harmless pictures of the German Reformation. What would people not do if some real psychologist told us about a genuine Luther — told us not with the moralist simplicity of a country priest, or the sweet and cautious modesty of a Protestant historian, but, say, with the fearlessness of a Taine, which springs from strength of character and not from a prudent toleration of strength? (The Germans, by the bye, have already produced the classic specimen of this toleration, and they may well count him as one of their own: Leopold Ranke, that born classical advocate of every causa fortior, that cleverest of all the clever opportunists.)

4.29.oldText: 20. But you will soon understand me. — In short, is there not reason enough for us psychologists never to get free of a certain mistrust of our own selves nowadays? Probably even we are still "too good" for our work. Whatever contempt we feel for this popular craze for morality, we are perhaps none the less its victims, its prey and its slaves; probably it infects even us. What was that diplomat warning us about, when he told his colleagues: "Let us especially mistrust our first impulses, gentlemen! they are almost always good"? This is how every psychologist should talk to his colleagues today. And so we return to our problem, which in fact demands a certain severity from us, a certain mistrust, especially of "first impulses." The ascetic ideal in the service of projected emotional excess: anyone who remembers the previous essay will already partly anticipate the essential meaning packed into these ten words. The thorough unhinging of the human soul, its plunge into terror, frost, ardor and rapture, so that it is freed, as by some lightning shock, from all the smallness and pettiness of unhappiness, depression and discomfort: what ways lead to this goal? And which of them leads there most safely?... At bottom all great emotions have this power, provided they find a sudden outlet — emotions such as rage, fear, lust, revenge, hope, triumph, despair, cruelty. And indeed the ascetic priest has had no scruples about enlisting the whole pack of hounds that rage in the human kennel, unleashing now these and now those. His aim is always the same: to wake man out of his protracted melancholy and chase away, at least for a time, his dull pain and shrinking misery, and always with a religious interpretation and justification to sanction it. Of course this emotional excess has to be paid for afterward — it makes the ill more ill — and so, by modern standards, this kind of remedy for pain is a "guilty" kind.

4.30.oldText: Fairness, however, demands that we stress all the more that this remedy is applied with a good conscience. The ascetic priest has prescribed it in the most implicit belief that it is useful and indispensable — often enough almost collapsing in the presence of the pain he created. Fairness also demands that we stress that the violent physiological revenges of such excesses, and perhaps even the mental disturbances, are not absolutely inconsistent with the general character of this remedy. As we showed previously, it is not meant to heal diseases but to fight the unhappiness of that depression, and its object was to ease and deaden that unhappiness. The object, then, was achieved. The keynote that let the ascetic priest make every kind of agonizing and ecstatic music play on the fibres of the human soul was, as everyone knows, the exploitation of the feeling of "guilt." I indicated the origin of this feeling in the previous essay — as a piece of animal psychology and nothing else: there we met the feeling of "guilt" in its crude state, as it were. Only in the hands of the priest, real artist that he was with the feeling of guilt, did it take shape — oh, what a shape! "Sin" — for that is the name of the new priestly version of the animal "bad-conscience" (the inverted cruelty) — has so far been the greatest event in the history of the diseased soul. In "sin" we find the most perilous and fatal masterpiece of religious interpretation. Imagine man, suffering from himself in some way or other, at any rate physiologically, perhaps like an animal shut up in a cage, unclear about the why and the wherefore! Imagine him in his desire for reasons (reasons bring relief), and again in his desire for remedies, for narcotics at last, as he consults one who knows even the occult — and see, lo and behold, his wizard, the ascetic priest, gives him a hint, the first hint about the "cause" of his trouble: he must search for it in himself, in his guiltiness, in a piece of the past, and he must understand his very suffering as a state of punishment. He has heard, he has understood, the unfortunate man: he is now in the plight of a hen with a line drawn round it. He never gets out of the circle of lines. The sick man has been turned into "the sinner" — and for a few thousand years now we have not been able to get away from the sight of this new invalid, "a sinner" — shall we ever get away from it? — wherever we look, there is the hypnotic gaze of the sinner, always moving in one direction (in the direction of guilt, the only cause of suffering); there is the evil conscience, this "greuliche thier," to use Luther's language; there is rumination over the past, a distorted view of action, the gaze of the "green-eyed monster" turned on all action; there is the wilful misunderstanding of suffering, its transvaluation into feelings of guilt and fear of retribution; there are the scourge, the hairy shirt, the starving body, contrition; there is the sinner breaking himself on the ghastly wheel of a restless and morbidly eager conscience; there are mute pain, extreme fear, the agony of a tortured heart, the spasms of an unknown happiness, the shriek for "redemption." In fact, with this system of procedure the old depression, dullness and fatigue were absolutely conquered, and life itself became very interesting again: awake, eternally awake, sleepless, glowing, burnt away, exhausted and yet not tired — such was the figure of man, "the sinner," once he was initiated into these mysteries. This grand old wizard of an ascetic priest, in his fight with depression, had clearly triumphed; his kingdom had come. Men no longer grumbled at pain, men panted after pain: "More pain! More pain!" So for centuries on end his acolytes and initiates shrieked their demand. Every emotional excess that hurt; everything that broke, overthrew, crushed, transported, ravished; the mystery of torture-chambers, the ingenuity of hell itself — all this was now discovered, divined and exploited, all this was put at the wizard's service, all this helped to bring about the triumph of his ideal, the ascetic ideal. "My kingdom is not of this world," he said, both at the beginning and at the end: had he still the right to talk like that? — Goethe has maintained that there are only thirty-six tragic situations: from that we would infer, if we did not know otherwise, that Goethe was no ascetic priest. He — knows more.

4.32.oldText: 22. Wherever the ascetic priest has gained the mastery, he has corrupted the health of the soul, and so he has also corrupted taste in artibus et litteris — he corrupts it still. "So?" I hope I shall be granted this "so"; at any rate, I am not going to prove it first. Here is one solitary indication. It concerns the arch-book of Christian literature, their real model, their "book-in-itself." The Græco-Roman world was splendid, and its splendor included books. Right in the midst of it, face to face with an ancient world of writings not yet fallen into decay and ruin, at a time when certain books were still there to be read, books we would now give half our literature to possess, the simplicity and vanity of Christian agitators (they are generally called Fathers of the Church) dared to declare: "We too have our classical literature, we do not need that of the Greeks." And meanwhile they proudly pointed to their books of legends, their letters of apostles and their apologetic tractlets, just as the English "Salvation Army" today wages its fight against Shakespeare and other "heathens" with an analogous literature. You already guess it: I do not like the "New Testament." It almost upsets me to stand so isolated in my taste about this valued, this over-valued Scripture; the taste of two thousand years is against me; but what does it matter! "Here I stand! I cannot help myself" — I have the courage of my bad taste. The Old Testament is quite another matter; all honor to the Old Testament! In it I find great men, a heroic landscape, and one of the rarest phenomena in the world, the incomparable naïveté of the strong heart; further still, I find a people. In the New, on the contrary, I find just a hostel of petty sects, pure rococo of the soul, twisting angles and fancy touches, nothing but conventicle air, not to forget an occasional whiff of bucolic sweetness that belongs to the epoch (and the Roman province) and is less Jewish than Hellenistic. Meekness and braggadocio cheek by jowl; an emotional garrulousness that almost deafens; passionate hysteria, but no passion; painful pantomime; here manifestly everyone lacked good breeding. How dare anyone make as much fuss about their little failings as these pious little fellows do! No one cares a straw about it — let alone God. And finally they actually wish to have "the crown of eternal life," all these little provincials! In return for what, if you please? For what end? Insolence cannot be carried any further. An immortal Peter! Who could stand him! Their ambition makes one laugh: the creature serves up his most personal life, his melancholies and common-or-garden troubles, cut and dried, as though the Universe itself were obliged to bother about them, for he never tires of wrapping up God Himself in the petty misery in which his troubles are involved. And what about the atrocious form of this chronic hobnobbing with God? This Jewish, and not merely Jewish, slobbering and clawing importunacy towards God! — There are little despised "heathen nations" in East Asia from whom these first Christians could have learned something worth learning, a little tact in worshiping; these nations do not allow themselves to say aloud the name of their God. This seems to me delicate enough; it is certain that it is too delicate, and not only for primitive Christians. For a contrast, just recall Luther, the most "eloquent" and insolent peasant Germany has had, and think of the Lutheran tone in which he felt most in his element during his tête-à-têtes with God. Luther's opposition to the mediæval saints of the Church (in particular, to "that devil's hog, the Pope") was, there is no doubt, at bottom the opposition of a boor. He was offended at the good etiquette of the Church, that worship-etiquette of the sacerdotal code, which lets only the initiated and the silent into the holy of holies and shuts the door against boors. These were definitely not to be allowed a hearing on this planet — but Luther the peasant simply wished it otherwise; as it was, it was not German enough for him. He wished to talk directly, to talk personally, to talk "straight from the shoulder" with his God. Well, he has done it. The ascetic ideal, you will guess, was at no time and in no place a school of good taste, still less of good manners — at best it was a school for sacerdotal manners: that is, it contains in itself something that was a deadly enemy to all good manners. Lack of measure, opposition to measure, it is itself a "non plus ultra."

4.34.oldText: With all their noisy agitator-babble, however, they get nowhere with me. These trumpeters of reality are bad musicians; their voices do not rise from the depths audibly enough, they are not the mouthpiece of the abyss of scientific knowledge — for today scientific knowledge is an abyss — and the word "science" in such trumpeter-mouths is a prostitution, an abuse, an impertinence. The truth is just the opposite of what the ascetic theory maintains. Science today has absolutely no belief in itself, let alone in an ideal above itself. And wherever science is still made of passion, love, ardor and suffering, it is not the opposite of the ascetic ideal but rather the incarnation of that ideal's latest and noblest form. Does that sound strange? There are plenty of brave and decent working people, even among the learned men of today, who like their little corner. Just because they are pleased to be there, they sometimes become indecently loud in demanding that people today should be quite content, especially in science — for in science there is so much useful work to do. I do not deny it. There is nothing I should like less than to spoil these honest workers' delight in their handiwork, for I rejoice in their work. But the fact that science requires hard work, and that it has contented workers, is no proof at all that science as a whole has one end, one will, one ideal, one passion for a great faith today. The contrary, as I have said, is the case. When science is not the latest manifestation of the ascetic ideal — and such cases are so rare, so select and so exquisite that they cannot affect the general judgment — science is a hiding-place for every kind of cowardice, disbelief, remorse, despectio sui, bad conscience. It is the very anxiety that springs from having no ideal, the suffering from the lack of a great love, the discontent with an enforced moderation. Oh, what does science not cover today? How much, at any rate, does it not try to cover? The diligence of our best scholars, their senseless industry, their burning the candle of their brain at both ends, their very mastery in their handiwork: how often is the real meaning of all that to keep themselves from continuing to see a certain thing? Science as a self-anæsthetic: do you know that? You wound them — everyone who associates with scholars experiences this — you sometimes wound them to the quick with a perfectly harmless word. When you think you are paying them a compliment, you embitter them beyond all bounds, simply because you lacked the finesse to work out what kind of customers you had to deal with: the sufferer kind (who won't own up even to themselves what they really are), the dazed and unconscious kind who have only one fear — coming to consciousness.

4.37.oldText: 26. Or does the whole of modern history, perhaps, show more confidence in life and in its ideals? Its loftiest pretension today is to be a mirror. It rejects all teleology and wants no more "proving." It disdains to play the judge, and shows its good taste in that. It asserts as little as it denies; it fixes, it "describes." All this is ascetic to a high degree, yet nihilistic to a much higher degree; make no mistake about this! In the historian you see a gloomy, hard, but determined gaze, the eye of an isolated North Pole explorer (perhaps so as not to look within, so as not to look back?). There is snow; life is silenced here; the last crows that caw here are called "whither?", "Vanity," "Nada." Nothing more flourishes or grows here, except at most the metapolitics of St. Petersburg and the "pity" of Tolstoi. Then there is that other school of historians, a perhaps still more "modern" school, voluptuous and lascivious, which ogles life and the ascetic ideal with equal fervor, which wears the word "artist" like a glove, and has by now secured a "corner" for itself in all the praise of contemplation. Oh, what a thirst these sweet intellectuals arouse, even for ascetics and winter landscapes! Nay! The devil take these "contemplative" folk! I would much rather wander with those historical Nihilists through the gloomiest, grey, cold mist! Nay, I shall not mind listening (supposing I have to choose) to someone completely unhistorical and anti-historical (a man like Dühring, for instance, whose periods have intoxicated a hitherto shy and unavowed species of "beautiful souls" in contemporary Germany, the species anarchistica within the educated proletariate). The "contemplative" are a hundred times worse. Nothing has ever made me so intensely nauseous as one of those "objective" chairs, one of those scented mannikins-about-town of history, a thing half-priest, half-satyr (Renan parfum). The high, shrill falsetto of his applause betrays what he lacks and where he lacks it: it betrays where the Fates, in his case, have plied their ghastly shears, alas! in too surgeon-like a fashion! I find this distasteful, and it tries my patience. Let him stay patient at such sights who has nothing to lose by it. For me the sight is enraging; such spectators embitter me against the "play," even more than the play itself does (history itself, you understand). Anacreontic moods come over me imperceptibly. This Nature, who gave the steer its horn and the lion its χάσμ ὀδοντων: for what purpose did Nature give me my foot? — To kick, by St. Anacreon, and not merely to run away! To trample on all the worm-eaten "chairs," the cowardly contemplators, the lascivious eunuchs of history, the flirters with ascetic ideals, the righteous hypocrites of impotence! All reverence from me to the ascetic ideal, in so far as it is honorable! So long as it believes in itself and plays no pranks on us! But I do not like all these coquettish bugs, whose insatiable ambition is to smell of the infinite until at last the infinite smells of bugs. I do not like the whited sepulchres with their stagey imitation of life. I do not like the tired and the used up who wrap themselves in wisdom and look "objective." I do not like the agitators dressed up as heroes, who hide their dummy-heads behind the stalking-horse of an ideal. I do not like the ambitious artists who would fain play the ascetic and the priest, and are at bottom nothing but tragic clowns. I do not like, again, these newest speculators in idealism, the Anti-Semites, who roll their eyes in the patent Christian-Aryan-man-of-honor fashion today, and with moralist attitudes and agitation dodges so cheap that they exhaust any patience, try to rouse all the blockhead elements in the populace (the unfailing success of every kind of intellectual charlatanism in present-day Germany is tied to the almost indisputable and already quite palpable desolation of the German mind. I look for its cause in a too exclusive diet of papers, politics, beer and Wagnerian music, not forgetting the condition this diet presupposes: the national exclusiveness and vanity, the strong but narrow principle "Germany, Germany above everything," and finally the paralysis agitans of "modern ideas"). Europe today is above all wealthy and ingenious in means of excitement; it apparently has no more pressing need than stimulantia and alcohol. Hence the enormous counterfeiting of ideals, those most fiery spirits of the mind; hence also the repulsive, evil-smelling, perjured, pseudo-alcoholic air everywhere. I should like to know how many cargoes of imitation idealism, of hero-costumes and high-falutin' claptrap, how many casks of sweetened pity liqueur (Firm: la religion de la souffrance), how many crutches of righteous indignation to prop up these flat-footed intellects, how many comedians of the Christian moral ideal would have to be exported from Europe today before its air smelled pure again. It is obvious that this over-production opens up a new trade possibility, and obvious that a new business is to be done in little ideal idols and obedient "idealists" — don't pass over this tip! Who has the courage? We hold in our hands the possibility of idealizing the whole earth. But what am I saying, courage? Here we need only one thing — a hand, a free, a very free hand.

4.38.oldText: 27. Enough! Enough! Let us leave these curiosities and complexities of the modern spirit, which provoke as much laughter as disgust. Our problem, the problem of the meaning of the ascetic ideal, can certainly do without them. What has it to do with yesterday or today? I shall deal with those matters more thoroughly and severely elsewhere (under the title "A Contribution to the History of European Nihilism"; I refer here to a work I am preparing: The Will to Power, an Attempt at a Transvaluation of All Values). I bring them up here for one reason only. Even in the most intellectual sphere, the ascetic ideal has at times just one real kind of enemies and damagers: the comedians of this ideal, because they awaken mistrust. Everywhere else the mind works seriously, powerfully and without counterfeiting, and there it dispenses altogether with an ideal (the popular name for this abstinence is "Atheism"), except for the will for truth. But this will, this remnant of an ideal, is, if you will believe me, that very ideal in its severest and cleverest formulation, esoteric through and through, stripped of all outworks; so it is not so much the ideal's remnant as its kernel. Unqualified honest atheism (and we, the most intellectual men of this age, breathe no other air) is not as opposed to that ideal as it seems. It is rather one of the last phases in the ideal's evolution, one of its syllogisms and pieces of inherent logic. It is the awe-inspiring catastrophe of a two-thousand-year training in truth, a training that finally forbids itself the lie of the belief in God. (India saw the same course of development, quite independently, and so with some demonstrative value: the same ideal driving to the same conclusion, with the decisive point reached five hundred years before the European era, or more precisely at the time of Buddha. It began in the Sankhyam philosophy, and Buddha then popularized it and made it into a religion.)

4.39.oldText: What has really triumphed over the Christian God? I ask the question with all strictness. The answer stands in my Joyful Wisdom, Aph. 357: "the Christian morality itself, the idea of truth taken with ever-increasing seriousness, the confessor-subtlety of the Christian conscience translated and sublimated into the scientific conscience, into intellectual cleanness at any price. To regard Nature as though it were a proof of the goodness and guardianship of God; to interpret history in honor of a divine reason, as a constant proof of a moral order of the world and a moral teleology; to explain our own personal experiences, as pious men have for long enough explained them, as though every arrangement, every nod, every single thing were invented and sent out of love for the salvation of the soul: all this is now done away with. The conscience is against it, and every subtler conscience regards it as disreputable, dishonorable, as lying, feminism, weakness, cowardice. By this severity, if by anything at all, we are good Europeans and heirs of Europe's longest and bravest self-mastery.". .. All great things bring about their own ruin by an act of self-dissolution: so wills the law of life, the law of necessary "self-mastery" even in the essence of life. The law-giver is always finally exposed to the cry, "patere legem quam ipse tulisti." So Christianity went to ruin as a dogma, through its own morality; and so Christianity must go to ruin again today as a morality. We are standing on the threshold of this event. Christian truthfulness draws one conclusion after another, and at last it draws its strongest conclusion, the one against itself. That happens when it puts the question: "what is the meaning of every will for truth?" And here I touch again on my problem, on our problem, my unknown friends (for as yet I know of no friends). What sense has our whole being, if not that in us that will for truth has become conscious of itself as a problem? — With this self-consciousness of the will for truth, morality from now on goes to pieces; there is no doubt about it. This is that great hundred-act play reserved for the next two centuries of Europe, the most terrible, the most mysterious, and perhaps also the most hopeful of all plays.

1.0.oldText: 1. We are unknown to ourselves, we knowers — and for good reason. We have never searched for ourselves, so how could we ever find ourselves? It has been rightly said: "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Our treasure is wherever the hives of our knowledge stand. We are always striving toward those hives, born as we are to flight, gatherers of the spirit's honey. In our hearts we care, truly, for only one thing — to bring something "home to the hive!"

1.1.oldText: As for the rest of life and its so-called "experiences" — which of us has any serious interest in them? Or sufficient time? When it comes to such matters, I'm afraid we are never properly present; our heart isn't there, and certainly not our ear. We are like a man who, lost in some divine distraction, or sunk in the seas of his own soul, suddenly wakes when the clock has just thundered all twelve strokes of noon in his ear, and asks himself, "What has just struck?" In the same way we sometimes rub our puzzled ears afterward and ask, in complete astonishment and embarrassment, "What have we just lived through?" And further: "Who in fact are we?" and we count, after they have struck, as I said, all the twelve throbbing beats of the clock of our experience, of our life, of our being — and we miscount in the attempt. Of necessity we remain strangers to ourselves, we do not understand ourselves, we cannot help but mistake ourselves, for of us the motto holds true to all eternity: "Each is farthest from himself" — as far as ourselves are concerned, we are not "knowers."

1.2.oldText: 2. My thoughts on the genealogy of our moral prejudices — for that is what is at stake in this polemic — found their first, blunt, provisional expression in that collection of aphorisms entitled Human, all-too-Human, a Book for Free Minds, which I began writing in Sorrento, during a winter that allowed me to gaze over the broad and dangerous territory my mind had wandered up to that point. This was in the winter of 1876-77; the thoughts themselves are older. In substance they were already the same thoughts I take up again in the following essays — we may hope that they have benefited from the long interval, that they have grown riper, clearer, stronger, more complete. But the fact that I still cling to them even now, that in the meantime they have only fastened more firmly to one another, have indeed grown out of their original shapes and into each other, all this strengthens in me the joyful confidence that they cannot have been originally separate, disconnected, capricious, or sporadic phenomena, but must have sprung from a common root, from a fundamental "fiat" of knowledge, whose empire reached to the soul's depths, and that grew ever more definite in its voice and in its demands. That is the only state of affairs that befits a philosopher.

1.3.oldText: We have no right to be "disconnected"; we must neither err "disconnectedly" nor strike at truth "disconnectedly." Rather, with the necessity with which a tree bears its fruit, our thoughts grow connected and interrelated — our values, our Yes's and No's and If's and Whether's — mutual witnesses of one will, one health, one kingdom, one sun. As to whether these fruits of ours are to your taste — but what does that matter to the trees? What does that matter to us, us philosophers?

1.4.oldText: 3. Owing to a scrupulousness peculiar to me, which I confess reluctantly — it concerns morality, after all — a scrupulousness that has shown itself in my life from such an early age, with such spontaneity, such chronic persistence, and such keen opposition to environment, epoch, precedent, and ancestry that I would have been almost entitled to call it my "a priori" — my curiosity and my suspicion were bound, soon enough, to halt at the question: what was actually the origin of our "Good" and our "Evil"? Indeed, at the boyish age of thirteen the problem of the origin of Evil already haunted me. At an age "when games and God divide one's heart," I devoted to that problem my first childish attempt at the literary game, my first philosophical essay — and as for my infantile solution to the problem, well, I quite properly gave the honor to God, and made him the father of evil. Did my own "a priori" demand that precise solution from me? That new, immoral, or at least "amoral" "a priori," and that "categorical imperative" which was its voice (oh, how hostile to the Kantian article, and how pregnant with problems!), to which since then I have given more and more attention — indeed, far more than mere attention. Fortunately I soon learned to separate theological from moral prejudices, and I gave up looking for a supernatural origin of evil. A certain amount of historical and philological education, to say nothing of an innate faculty of psychological discrimination par excellence, succeeded almost immediately in transforming my original problem into this one: under what conditions did Man invent for himself those judgments of values, "Good" and "Evil"? And what intrinsic value do they possess in themselves? Have they so far hindered or advanced human well-being? Are they a symptom of the distress, impoverishment, and degeneration of human life? Or, conversely, do they manifest the fullness, strength, and will of life — its courage, self-confidence, and future? On these questions I found and risked the most diverse answers in my mind; I distinguished between periods, peoples, and castes; I became a specialist in my own problem, and out of my answers grew new questions, new investigations, new conjectures, new probabilities — until at last I had a land of my own and a soil of my own, a whole secret world growing and flowering, like hidden gardens of whose existence no one could have an inkling. Oh, how happy we are, we finders of knowledge, provided we know how to keep silent long enough.

1.5.oldText: 4. My first impulse to publish some of my hypotheses concerning the origin of morality I owe to a clear, well-written, even precocious little book in which a perverse and vicious kind of moral philosophy (your real English kind) was definitely presented to me for the first time; and this attracted me — with that magnetic attraction inherent in whatever is diametrically opposed and antithetical to one's own ideas. The book was titled The Origin of the Moral Emotions; its author, Dr. Paul Rée; the year of its appearance, 1877. I might almost say that I have never read anything in which every single dogma and conclusion has called forth from me so emphatic a negation as did that book — though a negation untainted by either pique or intolerance. I referred accordingly, in season and out of season, in the previous works on which I was then working, to the arguments of that book — not to refute them (for what have I to do with mere refutations?) but to substitute, as is natural to a positive mind, a more probable theory for an improbable one, and occasionally no doubt one philosophical error for another. In that early period I gave, as I have said, the first public expression to those theories of origin to which these essays are devoted, but with a clumsiness which I was the last to conceal from myself, for I was as yet cramped, still without a special language for these special subjects, still frequently liable to relapse and to vacillation. To go into details, compare what I say in Human, all-too-Human, part i., about the parallel early history of Good and Evil, Aph. 45 (namely, their origin from the castes of the aristocrats and the slaves); similarly, Aph. 136 et seq., concerning the birth and value of ascetic morality; similarly, Aphs. 96, 99, vol. ii., Aph. 89, concerning the Morality of Custom, that far older and more original kind of morality which is toto cœlo different from the altruistic ethics (in which Dr. Rée, like all the English moral philosophers, sees the ethical "Thing-in-itself"); finally, Aph. 92. Similarly, Aph. 26 in Human, all-too-Human, part ii., and Aph. 112, the Dawn of Day, concerning the origin of Justice as a balance between persons of approximately equal power (equilibrium being the hypothesis of all contract, and consequently of all law); similarly, concerning the origin of Punishment, Human, all-too-Human, part ii., Aphs. 22, 23 — where the deterrent object is neither essential nor original (as Dr. Rée thinks); rather, this object is only imported, under certain definite conditions, and always as something extra and additional.

1.6.oldText: 5. In reality I had set my heart at that time on something far more important than the nature of the theories — my own or others' — concerning the origin of morality. (Or, more precisely: from my view, the real function of these theories was to point toward an end to which they were one means among many.) The issue for me was the value of morality, and on that subject I had to place myself in a state of abstraction in which I was almost alone with my great teacher Schopenhauer, to whom that book — with all its passion and inherent contradiction (for that book too was a polemic) — turned for present help, as though he were still alive. The issue, strangely enough, was the value of the "un-egoistic" instincts: the instincts of pity, self-denial, and self-sacrifice, which Schopenhauer had so persistently painted in golden colors, deified and etherealized, until at last they appeared to him, as it were, high and dry, as "intrinsic values in themselves," on the strength of which he uttered both to Life and to himself his own negation. But against these very instincts there voiced itself in my soul a more and more fundamental mistrust, a skepticism that dug ever deeper; and in this very instinct I saw the great danger of mankind, its most sublime temptation and seduction — seduction to what? to nothingness? In these very instincts I saw the beginning of the end: stagnation, the exhaustion that gazes backward, the will turning against Life, the last illness announcing itself with its own mincing melancholy. I realized that the morality of pity, which spread wider and wider, and whose grip infected even philosophers with its disease, was the most sinister symptom of our modern European civilization; I realized that it was the route along which that civilization slid on its way to — a new Buddhism? A European Buddhism? Nihilism? This exaggerated estimation in which modern philosophers have held pity is quite a new phenomenon: until then philosophers were absolutely unanimous on the worthlessness of pity. I need only mention Plato, Spinoza, La Rochefoucauld, and Kant — four minds as mutually different as is possible, but united on one point: their contempt of pity.

1.7.oldText: 6. This problem of the value of pity and of the pity-morality (I am an opponent of the modern infamous emasculation of our emotions) seems at first glance a mere isolated problem, a single question mark standing on its own. But anyone who once halts at this problem and learns how to put questions will experience what I experienced: a new and immense vista unfolds before him, a sense of potentiality seizes him like a vertigo, every species of doubt, mistrust, and fear springs up, the belief in morality — nay, in all morality — totters; finally a new demand voices itself. Let us speak this new demand out loud: we need a critique of moral values, the value of these values is for the first time to be called into question — and for this purpose a knowledge is necessary of the conditions and circumstances out of which these values grew, under which they evolved and were distorted (morality as a result, as a symptom, as a mask, as Tartuffism, as disease, as a misunderstanding; but also morality as a cause, as a remedy, as a stimulant, as a fetter, as a drug) — especially since such a knowledge has neither existed up to the present time nor is even now generally desired. The value of these "values" was taken for granted as an indisputable fact, beyond all question. No one has so far exhibited the faintest doubt or hesitation in judging the "good man" to be of higher value than the "evil man" — of higher value with regard specifically to human progress, utility, and prosperity, not forgetting the future. What? Suppose the converse were the truth! What? Suppose there lurked in the "good man" a symptom of retrogression — a danger, a temptation, a poison, a narcotic — by means of which the present battened on the future! More comfortable, perhaps, and less risky than its opposite, but also pettier, meaner! So that morality would really be saddled with the guilt if the maximum potentiality of the power and splendor of the human species were never to be attained? So that morality would really be the danger of dangers?

1.8.oldText: 7. Enough — once this vista had disclosed itself to me, I had reason to search for learned, bold, and industrious colleagues (I am still doing it to this very day). It means traversing, with new clamorous questions and at the same time with new eyes, the immense, distant, and completely unexplored land of morality — of a morality that has actually existed and been actually lived! And is this not practically equivalent to first discovering that land? If, in this context, I thought, among others, of the aforesaid Dr. Rée, I did so because I had no doubt that from the very nature of his questions he would be compelled to have recourse to a truer method in order to obtain his answers. Have I deceived myself on that score? At any rate I wished to give a better direction of vision to an eye of such keenness and such impartiality. I wished to direct him toward the real history of morality, and to warn him, while there was yet time, against a world of English theories that culminated in the blue vacuum of heaven. Other colors, of course, rise immediately to one's mind as being a hundred times more potent than blue for a genealogy of morals — for instance, gray, by which I mean authentic facts capable of definite proof and that have actually existed: in short, the whole of that long hieroglyphic script (so hard to decipher) about the past history of human morals. This script was unknown to Dr. Rée; but he had read Darwin — and so in his philosophy the Darwinian beast and that pink of modernity, the demure weakling and dilettante who "bites no longer," shake hands politely in a fashion that is at least instructive: the latter exhibiting a certain facial expression of refined and good-humored indolence, tinged with a touch of pessimism and exhaustion, as if it really did not pay to take all these things — moral problems, I mean — so seriously. I, on the other hand, think that there are no subjects which pay better for being taken seriously; part of this payment is that perhaps eventually they admit of being taken gaily. This gaiety indeed — or, to use my own language, this joyful wisdom — is a payment: a payment for a protracted, brave, laborious, burrowing seriousness, which, it goes without saying, is the attribute of but a few. But on the day when we say from the fullness of our hearts, "Forward! our old morality too is fit material for Comedy," we shall have discovered a new plot, a new possibility for the Dionysian drama entitled The Soul's Fate — and he will speedily make use of it, one can wager safely: he, the great ancient eternal dramatist of the comedy of our existence.

1.9.oldText: 8. If this writing is obscure to anyone, and grates on his ears, I do not think the blame is necessarily mine. It is clear enough, on the assumption I take for granted — namely, that the reader has first read my previous writings, and has not grudged them a certain amount of trouble: it is not, indeed, a simple matter to get really at their essence. Take, for instance, my Zarathustra: I allow no one to pass muster as knowing that book unless every single word in it has at some time wrought in him a profound wound, and at some time exercised on him a profound enchantment. Then and not till then can he enjoy the privilege of participating reverently in the halcyon element from which that work is born — in its sunny brilliance, its distance, its spaciousness, its certainty. In other cases the aphoristic form produces difficulty, but only because this form is treated too casually. An aphorism properly coined and cast into its final mold is far from being "deciphered" as soon as it has been read; on the contrary, it is then that it first requires to be expounded — and for that purpose an art of exposition is necessary. The third essay in this book provides an example of what I am offering, of what I call exposition in such cases: an aphorism is prefixed to that essay; the essay itself is its commentary. Certainly one quality which today has been best forgotten — and that is why it will take some time yet for my writings to become readable — is essential in order to practice reading as an art: a quality for the exercise of which it is necessary to be a cow, and under no circumstances a modern man! — rumination.

2.0.oldText: 1. Those English psychologists, who up to the present are the only philosophers we have to thank for any attempt to push toward a history of the origin of morality — these men, I say, offer us in their own personalities no paltry problem. Indeed, if I am to be quite frank about it, in their capacity as living riddles, they have an advantage over their books: they themselves are interesting! These English psychologists — what do they really mean? We always find them, voluntarily or involuntarily, at the same task: pushing to the front the partie honteuse of our inner world, and looking for the efficient, governing, and decisive principle in precisely that quarter where the intellectual self-respect of the race would be most reluctant to find it (for example, in the vis inertiæ of habit, or in forgetfulness, or in a blind and fortuitous mechanism and association of ideas, or in some factor that is purely passive, reflex, molecular, or fundamentally stupid) — what is the real motive power that always impels these psychologists in precisely this direction? Is it some sinister, vulgar, malignant instinct for human disparagement, perhaps incomprehensible even to itself? Or a touch of pessimistic jealousy, the mistrust of disillusioned idealists who have grown gloomy, poisoned, and bitter? Or some petty subconscious enmity and rancor against Christianity (and Plato), one that has conceivably never crossed the threshold of consciousness? Or just a vicious taste for whatever in life is bizarre, painfully paradoxical, mystical, and illogical? Or, as a final alternative, a dash of each of these motives — a little vulgarity, a little gloom, a little anti-Christianity, a little craving for the necessary piquancy?

2.1.oldText: But I am told that it is simply a case of old, frigid, and tedious frogs crawling and hopping around men and inside men, as if they were as thoroughly at home there as they would be in a swamp.

2.2.oldText: I oppose this statement; indeed, I do not believe it. And if, given the impossibility of knowledge, one is permitted to wish, then I wish from my heart that just the converse metaphor should apply — that these analysts, with their psychological microscopes, should be at bottom brave, proud, and magnanimous animals who know how to bridle both their hearts and their pains, and have specifically trained themselves to sacrifice what is desirable to what is true: any truth, in fact, even the simple, bitter, ugly, repulsive, unchristian, immoral truths — for there are truths of that description.

2.3.oldText: 2. All honor, then, to the noble spirits who would gladly dominate these historians of morality. But it is certainly a pity that they themselves lack the historical sense, that they are quite deserted by all the beneficent spirits of history. The whole train of their thought runs, as was always the way of old-fashioned philosophers, on thoroughly unhistorical lines: there is no doubt about that. The crass ineptitude of their genealogy of morals is immediately apparent the moment the question arises of ascertaining the origin of the idea and judgment of "good." "Originally," so runs their decree, "man praised and called 'good' altruistic acts from the standpoint of those on whom they were conferred — that is, those to whom they were useful; subsequently the origin of this praise was forgotten, and altruistic acts, simply because, as a matter of habit, they were praised as good, came also to be felt as good — as if they contained in themselves some intrinsic goodness." The thing is obvious: this initial derivation already contains all the typical and idiosyncratic traits of the English psychologists — we have "utility," "forgetting," "habit," and finally "error," the whole assemblage forming the basis of a system of values on which the higher man has up to the present prided himself, as though it were a kind of privilege of man in general. This pride must be brought low, this system of values must lose its values: is that achieved?

2.4.oldText: Now the first argument that comes ready to my hand is that the real homestead of the concept "good" is sought and located in the wrong place: the judgment "good" did not originate among those to whom goodness was shown. Much rather has it been the good themselves — that is, the aristocratic, the powerful, the high-stationed, the high-minded — who have felt that they themselves were good, and that their actions were good, that is to say of the first order, in contradistinction to all that was low, low-minded, vulgar, and plebeian. It was out of this pathos of distance that they first arrogated to themselves the right to create values for their own profit, and to coin the names of such values: what had they to do with utility? The standpoint of utility is as alien and inapplicable as it could possibly be when we have to deal with so volcanic an effervescence of supreme values, creating and demarcating as they do a hierarchy within themselves: it is at this juncture that one arrives at an appreciation of the contrast to that tepid temperature which is the presupposition on which every combination of worldly wisdom and every calculation of practical expediency is always based — and not for one occasional, not for one exceptional instance, but chronically. The pathos of nobility and distance, as I have said, the chronic and despotic esprit de corps and fundamental instinct of a higher dominant race coming into association with a meaner race, an "under race" — this is the origin of the antithesis of "good" and "bad."

2.5.oldText: (The masters' right of giving names goes so far that we are permitted to look upon language itself as the expression of the power of the masters: they say "this is that, and that," they seal finally every object and every event with a sound, and thereby at the same time take possession of it.) It is because of this origin that the word "good" is far from having any necessary connection with altruistic acts, contrary to the superstitious belief of these moral philosophers. On the contrary, it is on the occasion of the decay of aristocratic values that the antithesis between "egoistic" and "altruistic" presses more and more heavily on the human conscience — it is, to use my own language, the herd instinct that finds in this antithesis its expression in many ways. And even then it takes considerable time for this instinct to become sufficiently dominant for the valuation to be inextricably dependent on this antithesis (as is the case in contemporary Europe); for today that prejudice is predominant which, acting even now with all the intensity of an obsession and brain disease, holds that "moral," "altruistic," and "désintéressé" are concepts of equal value.

2.6.oldText: 3. In the second place, quite apart from the fact that this hypothesis as to the genesis of the value "good" cannot be historically upheld, it suffers from an inherent psychological contradiction. The utility of altruistic conduct has presumably been the origin of its being praised, and this origin has supposedly become forgotten — but in what conceivable way is this forgetting possible? Has perhaps the utility of such conduct ceased at some given moment? The contrary is the case. This utility has rather been experienced every day, at all times, and is consequently a feature that obtains a new and regular emphasis with every fresh day. It follows that, far from vanishing from consciousness, far indeed from being forgotten, it must necessarily become impressed on consciousness with ever-increasing distinctness. How much more logical is that contrary theory (it is not the truer for that) which is represented, for instance, by Herbert Spencer, who places the concept "good" as essentially similar to the concept "useful," "purposive," so that in the judgments "good" and "bad" mankind is simply summarizing and investing with a sanction its unforgotten and unforgettable experiences concerning the "useful-purposive" and the "mischievous-non-purposive." According to this theory, "good" is the attribute of that which has previously shown itself useful, and so is able to claim to be considered "valuable in the highest degree," "valuable in itself." This method of explanation is also, as I have said, wrong, but at any rate the explanation itself is coherent, and psychologically tenable.

2.7.oldText: 4. The signpost which first put me on the right track was this question: what is the true etymological significance of the various symbols for the idea "good" that have been coined in the various languages? I then found that they all led back to the same evolution of the same idea — that everywhere "aristocrat," "noble" (in the social sense) is the root idea, out of which there have necessarily developed "good" in the sense of "with aristocratic soul," "noble" in the sense of "with a soul of high calibre," "with a privileged soul" — a development that invariably runs parallel with that other evolution by which "vulgar," "plebeian," "low" are made to change finally into "bad." The most eloquent proof of this last contention is the German word "schlecht" itself: this word is identical with "schlicht" (compare "schlechtweg" and "schlechterdings"), which originally, and as yet without any sinister innuendo, simply denoted the plebeian man in contrast to the aristocratic man. It is at the sufficiently late period of the Thirty Years' War that this sense becomes changed to the sense now current. From the standpoint of the Genealogy of Morals this discovery seems to me substantial: the lateness of it is to be attributed to the retarding influence exercised in the modern world by democratic prejudice in the sphere of all questions of origin. This prejudice extends, as will shortly be shown, even into the province of natural science and physiology, which prima facie is the most objective. The extent of the mischief which this prejudice causes (once it is free of all trammels except those of its own malice), particularly to ethics and history, is shown by the notorious case of Buckle: it was in Buckle that that plebeianism of the modern spirit, which is of English origin, broke out once again from its malignant soil with all the violence of a slimy volcano, and with that salted, rampant, and vulgar eloquence with which up to the present time all volcanoes have spoken.

2.8.oldText: 5. With regard to our problem, which can justly be called an intimate one, and which elects to appeal to only a limited number of ears, it is of no small interest to ascertain that in those words and roots which denote "good" we catch glimpses of that arch-trait on the strength of which the aristocrats feel themselves to be beings of a higher order than their fellows. Indeed, in perhaps the most frequent instances they call themselves simply after their superiority in power (e.g. "the powerful," "the lords," "the commanders"), or after the most obvious sign of their superiority, as for example "the rich," "the possessors" (that is the meaning of arya; and the Iranian and Slavic languages correspond). But they also call themselves after some characteristic idiosyncrasy; and this is the case which now concerns us. They name themselves, for instance, "the truthful": this is first done by the Greek nobility, whose mouthpiece is found in Theognis, the Megarian poet. The word ἐσθλος, coined for the purpose, signifies etymologically "one who is," who has reality, who is real, who is true; and then with a subjective twist, the "true," as the "truthful": at this stage in the evolution of the idea, it becomes the motto and party cry of the nobility, and quite completes the transition to the meaning "noble," so as to place outside the pale the lying, vulgar man, as Theognis conceives and portrays him — until finally the word, after the decay of the nobility, is left to delineate psychological noblesse, and becomes as it were ripe and mellow. In the words κακός and δειλός (the plebeian in contrast to the ἀγαθός), cowardice is emphasized. This affords perhaps an inkling of the lines along which the etymological origin of the very ambiguous ἀγαθός is to be investigated. In the Latin malus (which I place side by side with μέλας) the vulgar man can be distinguished as the dark-colored, and above all as the black-haired ("hic niger est"), as the pre-Aryan inhabitants of the Italian soil, whose complexion formed the clearest mark of distinction from the dominant blondes, namely, the Aryan conquering race. At any rate Gaelic has afforded me the exact analogue — Fin (for instance, in the name Fin-Gal), the distinctive word of the nobility, finally meaning good, noble, clean, but originally the blond-haired man in contrast to the dark, black-haired aboriginals. The Celts, if I may make a parenthetic statement, were throughout a blond race; and it is wrong to connect, as Virchow still connects, those traces of an essentially dark-haired population which can be seen on the more elaborate ethnographic maps of Germany with any Celtic ancestry or with any admixture of Celtic blood: in this context it is rather the pre-Aryan population of Germany which surges up to these districts. (The same is true substantially of the whole of Europe: in point of fact, the subject race has finally again obtained the upper hand, in complexion and in shortness of skull, and perhaps in the intellectual and social qualities. Who can guarantee that modern democracy, still more modern anarchy, and indeed that tendency to the "Commune," the most primitive form of society, which is now common to all the Socialists in Europe, does not in its real essence signify a monstrous reversion — and that the conquering and master race, the Aryan race, is not also becoming inferior physiologically?) I believe I can explain the Latin bonus as the "warrior": my hypothesis is that I am right in deriving bonus from an older duonus (compare bellum = duellum = duen-lum, in which the word duonus appears to me to be contained). Bonus accordingly as the man of discord, of variance, "entzweiung" (duo), as the warrior: one sees what "the good" meant for a man in ancient Rome. Must not our actual German word gut mean "the godlike, the man of godlike race"? And be identical with the national name (originally the nobles' name) of the Goths?

2.9.oldText: The grounds for this supposition do not belong in this work.

2.10.oldText: 6. Above all, there is no exception (though there are opportunities for exceptions) to this rule: the idea of political superiority always resolves itself into the idea of psychological superiority, in those cases where the highest caste is at the same time the priestly caste, and in accordance with its general characteristics confers on itself the privilege of a title which alludes specifically to its priestly function. It is in these cases, for instance, that "clean" and "unclean" first confront each other as badges of class distinction; here again there develops a "good" and a "bad," in a sense which has ceased to be merely social. Moreover, care should be taken not to take these ideas of "clean" and "unclean" too seriously, too broadly, or too symbolically: all the ideas of ancient man have, on the contrary, got to be understood in their initial stages, in a sense which is, to an almost inconceivable extent, crude, coarse, physical, and narrow, and above all essentially unsymbolical. The "clean man" is originally only a man who washes himself, who abstains from certain foods that are conducive to skin diseases, who does not sleep with the unclean women of the lower classes, who has a horror of blood — not more, not much more! On the other hand, the very nature of a priestly aristocracy shows the reasons why, just at such an early juncture, there should ensue a really dangerous sharpening and intensification of opposed values: it is, in fact, through these opposed values that gulfs are cleft in the social plane which a veritable Achilles of free thought would shudder to cross. There is from the outset a certain diseased taint in such sacerdotal aristocracies, and in the habits which prevail in such societies — habits which, averse as they are to action, constitute a compound of introspection and explosive emotionalism, as a result of which there appears that introspective morbidity and neurasthenia which adheres almost inevitably to all priests at all times. With regard, however, to the remedy which they themselves have invented for this disease — the philosopher has no option but to state that it has proved itself in its effects a hundred times more dangerous than the disease, from which it should have been the deliverer. Humanity itself is still diseased from the effects of the naïvetés of this priestly cure. Take, for instance, certain kinds of diet (abstention from flesh), fasts, sexual continence, flight into the wilderness (a kind of Weir-Mitchell isolation, though of course without that system of excessive feeding and fattening which is the most efficient antidote to all the hysteria of the ascetic ideal); consider too the whole metaphysic of the priests, with its war on the senses, its enervation, its hair-splitting; consider its self-hypnotism on the fakir and Brahman principles (it uses Brahman as a glass disc and obsession), and that climax — only too easy to understand — of an unusual satiety with its panacea of nothingness (or God: the demand for a unio mystica with God is the demand of the Buddhist for nothingness, Nirvana — and nothing else!). In sacerdotal societies every element is on a more dangerous scale, not merely cures and remedies but also pride, revenge, cunning, exaltation, love, ambition, virtue, morbidity. Furthermore, it can fairly be stated that it is on the soil of this essentially dangerous form of human society — the sacerdotal form — that man really becomes for the first time an interesting animal, that in this form the soul of man has in a higher sense attained depths and become evil — and those are the two fundamental forms of the superiority that man has so far exhibited over every other animal.

2.11.oldText: 7. The reader will already have surmised with what ease the priestly mode of valuation can branch off from the knightly aristocratic mode, and then develop into the very antithesis of the latter: special impetus is given to this opposition by every occasion when the castes of the priests and warriors confront each other with mutual jealousy and cannot agree over the prize. The knightly-aristocratic "values" are based on a careful cult of the physical, on a flowering, rich, even effervescing healthiness that goes considerably beyond what is necessary for maintaining life — on war, adventure, the chase, the dance, the tourney — on everything, in fact, that is contained in strong, free, joyous action. The priestly-aristocratic mode of valuation is — as we have seen — based on other hypotheses: it is bad enough for this class when it is a question of war! Yet the priests are, as is notorious, the worst enemies — why? Because they are the weakest. Their weakness causes their hate to expand into a monstrous and sinister shape, a shape which is most crafty and most poisonous. The really great haters in the history of the world have always been priests, who are also the cleverest haters — in comparison with the cleverness of priestly revenge, every other piece of cleverness is practically negligible. Human history would be too fatuous a thing for words were it not for the cleverness imported into it by the weak — take at once the most important instance. All the world's efforts against the "aristocrats," the "mighty," the "masters," the "holders of power," are negligible by comparison with what has been accomplished against those classes by the Jews — the Jews, that priestly nation which eventually realized that the one method of effecting satisfaction on its enemies and tyrants was by means of a radical transvaluation of values, which was at the same time an act of the cleverest revenge. Yet the method was only appropriate to a nation of priests, to a nation of the most jealously nursed priestly revengefulness. It was the Jews who, in opposition to the aristocratic equation (good = aristocratic = beautiful = happy = loved by the gods), dared with a terrifying logic to suggest the contrary equation, and indeed to maintain with the teeth of the most profound hatred (the hatred of weakness) this contrary equation, namely: "the wretched are alone the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly, are alone the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome, are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed, for them alone is salvation — but you, on the other hand, you aristocrats, you men of power, you are to all eternity the evil, the horrible, the covetous, the insatiate, the godless; eternally also shall you be the unblessed, the cursed, the damned!" We know who it was who reaped the heritage of this Jewish transvaluation. In the context of the monstrous and inordinately fateful initiative which the Jews have exhibited in connection with this most fundamental of all declarations of war, I remember the passage which came to my pen on another occasion (Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 195) — that it was, in fact, with the Jews that the revolt of the slaves begins in the sphere of morals; that revolt which has behind it a history of two millennia, and which at the present day has only moved out of our sight because it — has achieved victory.

2.12.oldText: 8. But you do not understand this? You have no eyes for a force which has taken two thousand years to achieve victory? There is nothing wonderful in this: all lengthy processes are hard to see and to grasp. But this is what took place: from the trunk of that tree of revenge and hate — Jewish hate — that most profound and sublime hate, which creates ideals and changes old values into new creations, the like of which has never been on earth — there grew a phenomenon equally incomparable, a new love, the most profound and sublime of all kinds of love; and from what other trunk could it have grown? But beware of supposing that this love has soared on its upward growth as in any way a real negation of that thirst for revenge, as an antithesis to the Jewish hate! No, the contrary is the truth! This love grew out of that hate, as its crown, as its triumphant crown, circling wider and wider amid the clarity and fullness of the sun, and pursuing in the very kingdom of light and height its goal of hatred, its victory, its spoil, its strategy, with the same intensity with which the roots of that tree of hate sank into everything that was deep and evil with increasing stability and increasing desire. This Jesus of Nazareth, the incarnate gospel of love, this "Redeemer" bringing salvation and victory to the poor, the sick, the sinful — was he not really temptation in its most sinister and irresistible form, temptation to take the tortuous path to those very Jewish values and those very Jewish ideals?
